I have the honour to inform the house that I have received the following message:-
Ottawa, May 29, 1936.
Sir,

I have the honour to inform you that the Right Honourable Sir Lyman P. Duff, Chief Justice of Canada, acting as deputy of His Excellency the Governor General, will proceed to the Senate chamber on Tuesday next, second June, at 9 p.m., for the purpose of giving the royal assent to certain bills.
F. L. C. Pereira,
Assistant Secretary to the Governor General.
Mr. VIEN presented the first report of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

Hon. FERNAND RINFRET (Secretary of State) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 78, to amend The Dominion Elections Act, 1934.
He said: The purpose of this bill is to provide for the taking of votes at dominion byelections. It follows a bill passed previously at this session which postponed the annual revision of the list, and is to meet the representations of certain members of parliament that we were not providing for by-elections. I may add that the bill is in conformity with the recommendations of the special committee of the house. It is to be accompanied by a companion bill amending the Dominion Franchise Act, which must be preceded by a resolution, which resolution also appears on the order paper.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Hon. FERNAND RINFRET (Secretary of State) moved that the house go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Dominion Franchise Act, 1934, with respect to by-elections and to make provision for the appointment of enumerators and other necessary officers and for the preparation and printing of voters' lists and other necessary documents.
He said: His Excellency the Governor General, having been made acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the favourable consideration of the 'house.
Motion agreed to.

Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved that the house go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Judges Act to provide salaries for the Ontario appeal and high court judges as presently constituted; and further provide that when a vacancy occurs in the office of chief justice in appeal the office shall be abolished and the court shall thereafter consist of a chief justice and seven other judges.
He said: His Excellency the Governor General, having been made acquainted with the

The house resumed from Thursday, May 28, consideration in committee of Bill No. 61, to amend the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, 1932-Mr. Dunning-Mr. Johnston (Lake Centre) in the chair.
On section 6-Power to invest in stocks of other insurance companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: When the house rose last night we were discussing section 6 of this bill and I undertook to have the section further reviewed in order to make sure of its true effect. I have done so and am now able to advise the committee that under the section as it at present stands in the law a fire insurance company, having invested more than 15 per cent of its assets in common stocks, could under section 61 as it now stands invest further amounts in the common shares o' another insurance company, even if those shares did not comply as to dividends with subsection 1 of section 60. This, it is believed, was not the original intention and even if it was it should be changed. The amendment will make it clear that the concession made by section 61 will not apply to any company which has already invested more than 15 per cent of its assets in common stocks. I think that answers the question raised by the leader of the opposition last evening in connection with this section.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: I would hardly agree with the construction placed on the section as it stands, but that is unimportant; I cannot think that that is the meaning of it as it now stands. But why is subsection 2 added, "certain investments excepted"? It will be observed that this is a new section entirely and it provides that investments made after 1927 and before the first day of January of this year, under the provisions of so and so, shall not be deemed to be investments in common stocks within the meaning of subsections 6 and 7 of section 60. That brings it down to the first of this year and to all intents and purposes renders nugatory the provisions of the law in respect of common stocks since 1927 up to date.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932

The intention of subsection 2 is to avoid any interference with investments which have been made under the provisions of the act after 1927 down to date. I am advised they are very small, but in the absence of subsection 2 there would
be very grave question as to how the companies would stand in relation to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: This section is for the purpose of bringing within the penalty section of the act dominion companies, incorporated for purposes other than the transaction of insurance business, which nevertheless do transact that business. The act heretofore has applied only to companies incorporated for the purpose of carrying on the business of insurance, and it was never contemplated that any company not incorporated for that purpose, still less any company prohibited by its letters patent from transacting that business, would ever engage in it. Cases have arisen, however, where this has been done, and it is considered advisable to make such companies subject to the same penalty as now applies to a registered company which violates any provision of the act.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
That would not extend, I take it, to commercial corporations that provide benefits for their employees who make contributions to it, supplemented by a contribution from the company. Sometimes they are in the habit of referring to the employees as being insured in the company. Of course a joint stock company cannot lawfully carry on insurance, and if a change were made against them under the provisions of this section with a view of imposing a penalty, they would at once plead that the Joint Stock Companies Act provided that they should not have those powers conferred upon them, and this section would be wholly illusory as far

as the imposition of any penalty is concerned. You can put in the provision if you wish. It cannot have any effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: I think my right hon. friend will remember some cases during the last two or three years where in the absence of penalty provisions they just simply go on and do it anyway.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
But they cannot write
insurance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: They do it.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: No, but it is ultra vires.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: The question is, what to do to them about it.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: The answer is, cancel their charters under the Joint Stock Companies Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: This action we are proposing to take to-day will make penalties available for that offence.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Under the law as it stands, the directors would be liable if they are doing business that is ultra vires.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
The former Secretary
of State is not in the house. I have here a letter from him to the former Minister of Finance in which he makes that very point, that no penalty accrues in such a case.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: I know there is no penalty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: And he suggests in the letter that the proper method of dealing with it would be to create penalties under the insurance act which would apply in such cases. In fact, the whole situation arises out of one particular case-

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: -in western Canada, of which we found duplicates elsewhere, but not on so large a scale. The matter has been under consideration by the department of the Secretary of State from the standpoint of company incorporation and liability of directors, and by the Department of Insurance. The Department of Justice has also gone into the matter. I could read the letter, but I think I have fairly summarized it.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I think I know in a
general way what it is. Perhaps I have not made my point clear. Obviously a company incorporated under the provisions of the Joint Stock Companies Act of Canada could not transact the business of life insur-

Canadian and British Insurance
ance; that is a prohibited business under the statute. Therefore, if a charge were brought against such a company alleging that it had been transacting life insurance business, the plea would be that it had no such power under its charter. That would be clear. That is the point, T think, that has not been made plain. Here is a recognition of a legal right which they do not possess. That is my point. Look at the section;
Any company, or any other corporation incorporated under the laws of the Dominion of Canada or of the late province of Canada, or any fraternal society so incorporated, which, or any person who, acting on behalf of a company or such a corporation or society, transacts any class of insurance business in respect of which the company or such corporation or society is not registered under this act ...
That is a recognition of its right to do the business, which obviously it has not. It is under the statute a prohibited class of business, yet, being prohibited, we now recognize it for the purpose of punishing it. With all deference I say to the minister that that is a perfectly clear position. Now that the minister has brought it to my attention I do recall something of the matter to which he refers. But I never recognized for a moment the right of that company to carry on an insurance business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
We do not admit that we are doing so.
Mr. BENNETT; Quite so, but this says so. You say that any company which does this particular business is going to be punished. You cannot approbate and reprobate at the same time. My contention is that that is a prohibited business for a joint stock company. Being prohibited, obviously we cannot say: If you do the prohibited thing we are going to fine you under the insurance act. If the company goes beyond its charter it runs the risk of losing its charter, because what it does is ultra vires; the directors who transact the business are personally liable, and those who purport to receive the alleged benefits under it in fact receive none, because the business is not within the scope of the corporation. I do not think the section is happily drawn. It should be changed to read that any company "purporting" to transact the business, and so on, and refer it back to the provisions of the statute which makes it prohibited business. There is a general clause in the insurance act providing penalties for doing that which is prohibited by the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Well, this is prohibited by the act. The insurance act prohibits this
class of company from doing that business. All joint stock companies are so prohibited. I think we should say "purporting to transact insurance business," rather than recognize that they are doing it. That, I think, is the usual custom in drafting legislation of this kind. In other words they are holding themselves out as entitled to do something which they have no legal right to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Quite so.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: We are agreed as to that. But under the law as it stands there is a prohibition against their doing this thing under their charter. Therefore, it strikes me, all we have to do is to insert "purporting" to carry on business which they are not authorized to do; and we are going to punish them in this way rather than the other. That is all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Of course my right hon. friend understands that they are not a company within the definition of this act.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Certainly I do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: A corporation, within the definition of this act, means any corporation incorporated for the purpose of carrying on the business of insurance.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: That is my whole point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: The point is a legal one, and, again speaking with deference as a layman, when I get a report which has run the gauntlet of the department of the Secretary of State and the lawyers who have to do with company law, who suggest that with regard to this practice it is far better to amend the insurance act than to amend the companies act; when, having got that, the superintendent of insurance takes the matter up with the Department of Justice, and all the lawyers who have anything to do with it there suggest this course, what is a poor lay minister of finance to do?

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Do what his advisers tell him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
He can do very little else under the circumstances. The advice is legal advice, advice from the Deputy Minister of Justice:
In reply to your letter of the 2nd instant,
I may say that it does not appear that proceedings could be taken successfully under either the Companies Act or the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, 1932, in this case, and it may be somewhat doubtful if the letters patent of the above association could be cancelled if proceedings to that effect were taken.
In view of the above circumstances, it is suggested that section 111 of the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, 1932, as enacted by section 32 of chapter 27 of the



Canadian arid British Insurance
statutes of 1934, be amended to cover a company which was not incorporated for the purpose of carrying on the business of insurance, and if this amendment is approved, then it would be probably advisable to also amend section 142, as enacted by chapter 27 of 1934, and section 58 of the Foreign Insurance Companies Act, 1932, as enacted by section 28 or chapter 36 of the statutes of 1934. If you approve of these amendments, I would suggest that they be included in two new bills, and for this purpose, I herewith enclose drafts of such bills.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: These are not the sections referred to; they do not cover those two paragraphs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: But they do consist of the drafts sent for the purpose, enclosed with the letter I have just read.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: They are not so numbered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: The numbers have been changed, of course.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
But section 3, to which the letter referred, is another section. I still think, notwithstanding the opinion of the Department of Justice, that attention has not been directed to the point I am endeavouring to make. In connection with a companies act you will always find a disposition not to amend it along the lines that have been suggested in that communication, for reasons that are fairly obvious. The Department of State has certain obligations in connection with the granting of letters patent and there is always a desire to avoid as far as possible the determination antecedently of questions such as those now raised. I think in any event a writ of scire facias would cancel such letters patent, though I say that with difiidence because I have not looked it up. On the other hand, as far as this is concerned all the minister has to do is look at it. It reads:
Any company, or any other corporation incorporated under the laws of the Dominion of Canada or of the late province of Canada, or any fraternal society so incorporated, which, or any person who, acting on behalf of a company or such a corporation or society, transacts any class of insurance business in respect of which the company or such corporation or society is not registered-
If you charge them with that before a magistrate they may say, "That is nonsense; we are not doing that at all. We have no power to do it. It is ultra vires of our incorporation, and you cannot punish us for that. That is an imaginary offence."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Would it not be a matter of fact?

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
But the question of fact is this: These people say, "This is not the kind of insurance you are talking about at

all. We have no power to do that, and as we have no power to do it there can be no offence because we are not doing anything we have not power to do." The minister would not need to be a lawyer to raise that defence successfully before a magistrate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: But they advertise; they issue policies.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: But of what?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Insurance.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: If the minister says that-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: There is no doubt about it.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: But the point is not entirely without authority. There are authorities on questions of ultra vires business. I am not going to do other than have the minister make the explanation and say that he is bound by the opinion of those whose duty it is to advise him, but the records of the courts have shown frequently-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
One thing that does
astonish me is that this point, if it has any force, escaped the eagle eye of the law officer of the senate. This bill came from the senate, and had a pretty thorough grilling before the senate banking and commerce committee, which includes a great many lawyers, I believe. My right hon. friend will forgive me if I prefer to stay with what I have now in the way of advice, under the circumstances.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I say the minister is
bound to accept that opinion. I also point out to him, however, that ordinarily to pick up this section you would say it was to punish people who tried to carry on the business of insurance when they should not do so. I am only pointing out that if I were acting for the man thus charged I would simply say, "There cannot be any offence, because that is prohibited under our act of incorporation, and we are not doing anything more than we are permitted to do." Under our Companies Act these returns are made every year, and no one is charged with doing business that is ultra vires; but I am not raising the question. It is always well to remember what the minister said the other day, that there is nothing more uncertain than the ultimate determination of litigation. Sometimes it is determined by a point that has been raised without thought as to the effect or seriousness of it. I am not for a moment saying that the point is serious; I am only saying that when I read it I was struck with the thought that it was a situation that was rather anomalous, to charge a man with the commission of an offence when he says, "What I am doing cannot possibly be

Canadian and British Insurance
an offence for it is what I am forbidden to do under the statute, and I have been maintaining my position under the statute." Then you take another statute altogether, not related to the one under which he operates, and say he is carrying on the business of insurance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
It would be a pretty
ingenious defence, at any rate, would it not?

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I would not say that,
but since the minister is bound to accept the opinion of his law officers, I have nothing further to say on the point.

Section agreed to.
On section 17-Reserve liability for determining assets in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932

There is only a clerical
change here.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: When this -bill was before the house some years ago I suggested, and I do so again, that it is very desirable not to risk the whole machinery of the department on the accuracy of referring to a particular section. It is much easier to say "the provisions of this -act" than to name a particular section. Now we have before us sections which have taken up the time of two houses of parliament; which have been printed for the two houses of parliament; which have been repealed and reenacted, and what have we done? We have added three words here and perhaps only two words there. As I said to my colleagues at that time, although the draftsman did not think it desirable to follow my advice, all that it is necessary is to say is "notwithstanding anything contained in this act," and so on. That has been the usual way of drafting these bills. The moment you name a particular section and then amend by striking out a section and renumbering the rest you are up against that condition. I do think it is a waste of very excellent effort to have to check up these matters every session. It imposes too much of a burden upon the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
It is likely also to lead
to very serious complications in practice.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
That was just what I said a moment ago. The minister will perhaps remember that we were confronted with that situation at one time, as the superintendent of insurance may recall. In the course of an endeavour to number the sections they became confused, and we had a very considerable

amount of difficulty. It will be remembered that we were charged with grievous offences because we endeavoured to remedy the situation in a particular way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: I think I should make an explanation here, because this is new. Section 19 makes it possible for the minister to require from provincial companies registered or to be registered under the dominion act an undertaking that they will comply with that section of the act respecting the division of participating profits between policyholders and shareholders. Up to 1932 provincial companies registered under the dominion act were subject to that provision, but since 1932 they have been exempt from it at least in respect of business written since that date. Should the undertaking now provided for be given and then violated the penalty will be the cancellation of the certificate of registration.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: I think that is highly desirable. I do not desire to engage in a discussion of the matter to-day, but the 25 per cent that has to be made available to policyholders in my judgment is entirely too low.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Ninety per cent, is it not?

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: No, I am talking about another matter. Not less than 25 per cent of the profits must be made available for the surplus of the policyholders until such time as that surplus reaches a certain definite point. That was one of the provisions we passed today. If my personal views were to prevail 1 would make it a much larger percentage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: That is in the case of fire insurance companies?

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: I am dealing with the sections we have passed to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I did not refer to it
because it was merely correcting one of the section numbers.

speechtext:
What it did was to reenact the provision about the twenty-five per cent. The minister will find that:
(2) Subject to the payment of preferential dividends in accordance with subsection four of section ninety-nine of this act, until the surplus of the company shall equal or exceed the said liabilities in respect of all outstanding unmatured policies not reinsured, the company shall at the end of each year appropriate towards the surplus of such company at least twenty-five per centum of the profits of the company for the year last past.
Had I my way I think I would make that percentage larger, but I am quite conscious

Canadian and British Insurance
of the limitation imposed on the utilization of profits, ten per cent only being available for shareholders; that is, the shareholders' profits under the law as it now stands cannot be more than ten per cent of the profits earned. The law also goes further; there is a second branch-twenty-five per cent at least of the earned surplus must be appropriated to the policyholders.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932

speechtext: Yes, that is the complement of the provision with respect to shareholders' profits in life insurance companies. This provision in section 19 I think is not only highly desirable, but absolutely essential if we are to give provincial companies the status they would derive from having a certificate, because it would place other companies at a serious disadvantage if they were to be able to secure the certificate which had involved an attorning to our jurisdiction entirely in the one case and only partially in the other. In fact I thought it was done a year ago but apparently it was not.

Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Marine) moved the second reading of Bill No. 68, respecting the carriage of goods by water.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is to repeal the present Water-Carriage of Goods Act and replace it by a new statute which follows almost exactly the British carriage of goods by water act. The only differences between this and the British act are in such wording in the latter as is not applicable to Canada.
The British act was the outcome of the Brussels conference of 1922 when twenty-four maritime nations met there for the purpose of drafting a uniform carriage of goods by water act. Following this convention, Great Britain passed an act in 1924, and the United States some two months ago also passed an act which was modelled almost entirely on the British act. Canada was not a party to the Brussels convention, but by correspondence with Great Britain and the United

States we have been committed for a year or two to pass legislation making our act uniform with the others.
In addition to the situation as affecting uniformity there are other reasons for passing this bill. The old carriage of goods by water act is rather vague and indefinite and has been the cause of a good deal of litigation, whereas the new act is very clear and definite, and since it has been in force in England the litigation under it has fallen to a minimum.
The necessity for change was made apparent particularly in connection with the decision in the Sarniadoc case, which was carried to the privy council. Since that case was decided shipping interests in Canada have had considerable doubt as to whether it would be possible for them to insure against risks that properly should be insurable. The clause in question is the clause in the old act that makes it a condition that the ship must be seaworthy in every respect.
Section 3 is the only section about which there has been any trouble.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Yes. The present act does not include lumber in the definition of goods, and it has been very difficult for lumber interests, particularly in British Columbia, to obtain marine insurance on lumber shipped to the old country. There was one case in which a ship left British Columbia with a part cargo of lumber and took on additional cargo at Newport News. The lumber was damaged in transit and the American shipper was able to recover the insurance whereas the Canadian shipper was not. This bill corrects that situation and includes lumber in the definition of goods.
The legislation will also relieve the coasting trade by making it possible to avoid making out a bill of lading in all cases. It allows a simpler contract in coastwise shipping. It also relieves the obligation of having to guarantee the weight of bulk cargoes where the weight is determined by a third party.
I think that covers the essential points. Other points will arise in committee, but I may say that we have had representations from almost every unit of the water carriers' interests in Canada and there has been no serious opposition whatever to the bill, although its contents have been known for some time. It seems an obvious piece of legislation and one that is very much required.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston (Lake Centre) in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We had a letter from the Vancouver Merchants' Exchange, as I recall, asking for information about it. There is one other point. About two or three years ago, maybe longer, there was a dispute between the shippers and the carriers of goods. I recall part of the dispute, and it was based upon what is apparently being dealt with here; that is, the wide allowance of immunity that is extended to carriers of goods, and the difficulty of shippers in securing compensation through the courts. That was applicable not only to the carriage of goods by water act of Canada as it then stood, but also to the shipment of goods to the old country in carriers under the Water Carriage of Goods Act of Great Britain, upon which this new bill is modelled. While I am not desirous of hindering the passage of this legislation or of complaining about it, I should like to have had the opportunity of hearing from the Pacific coast and considering and presenting whatever representations they have to make.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I am advised by my officers that yesterday we received representations from the Vancouver Merchants' Exchange with a strong recommendation that lumber should be included. We were able to advise them that lumber was included and hoped that the bill would satisfy them.

That I think would probably cover the situation. I certainly do not wish to interfere with the passing of the bill, but I am most anxious that this important section of the export trade should be adequately covered.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Contract not to imply seaworthy ship.

Would the minister explain this section? Does it mean that there is no obligation upon the carrier to provide a seaworthy boat, and that if the stuff is lost he can say to the shipper, "That is your trouble"? What protection does the shipper have? He has no knowledge of the condition of the ship; he cannot go into that. What is his protection?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will turn to
paragraph 3 on the opposite page of the bill he will find an explanation of the obligation of the ship owner as to responsibility for the ship. If the accident occurs because of the unseaworthiness of the ship the ship owner is liable, but unseaworthiness cannot be pleaded unless the action arise because of that unseaworthiness.

Mr. Chairman, this is the only section upon which I wish to make a few observations. The minister knows that we in Canada have been very reluctant to pass this statute. It lessens very materially the burden of the ship owner. It represents the high point of the influence of shipping in Great Britain. The Brussels conference was the triumph of the great shipping interests over, shall I say, the agitation that commenced in the days of Plimsoll and was maintained with varying degrees of success until this final action was taken. Far be it from me to say it is absolutely unfair because that would not be the proper way in which to describe it. But in two or three particulars it very greatly changes our conception of responsibility on the part of the ship owner.
The minister will recall the circumstances that led to the enactment of the drastic legislation in connection with the seaworthiness of ships, ships in the fall of the year overladen, laden far beyond their proper depth, and going out to sea heavily insured, which finally culminated in that historic scene in the House of Commons when Mr. Plimsoll completely lost his head and was escorted out of the chamber in a desperate physical condition. But the result of the breakdown of Mr. Plimsoll was that Plimsoll's mark appears on every ship that leaves a British port. That of course has only to do with the depth to

Carriage of Goods by Water
which the ship is loaded, and with conditions under which the seamen are provided with food and other necessities while on the articles of the vessel.
Section 3 of this bill says:
There shall not be implied in any contract for the carriage of goods by water to which the rules apply any absolute undertaking by the carrier of the goods to provide a seaworthy ship.
The law as it developed was that in all contracts for carriage there was an implied condition, and that implied condition was the basis upon which, on the one hand, the owners of the cargo relied for assurance of the ship being in a condition of seaworthiness to carry the cargo, and, on the other hand, the crews relied upon it, feeling that there was no risk of life involved so far as the seaworthiness of the vessel was concerned.
The minister has not forgotten the terrible disaster which happened off the United States coast to a southbound British ship or the serious loss of life involved in the disaster to a northbound ship which was destroyed by fire off the coast of New Jersey. The question of liability is always a question of fact, determined as it was in those days by the question of seaworthiness. But now we have the word "absolute" inserted. It still maintains the principle upon which the law was predicated, that is, there is an implied contract of seaworthiness but not of absolute seaworthiness. When the minister said that this lessened litigation, I would say that while it is true it has lessened litigation because the British commercial interests do not have recourse to litigation except where great principles are involved, but rely upon arbitration-the great interests of the city of London determine questions of this kind not by reference to the courts except where great principles are involved, when they have recourse to the House of Lords-yet it has always seemed to me that this is rather a dangerous section, and I shall content myself with making that statement of my position. When you have regard to the enormous amount of traffic that is handled on the inland seas of this country-I do not think it affects so much shipping from our great seaports because sooner or later the ship will have Plimsoll's mark and be subject to the survey of the board of trade; if she is insured by Lloyd's there will be a survey, and if she is insured by other companies there will be a survey and the question of seaworthiness will always be considered. But when you come to our great lakes and to the question of the loading of the ship and the transporting of cargoes in the fall it is another matter. The

minister referred to the Sarniadoc case as an outstanding illustration of recent occurrence about which there was much litigation. We now have Canada engrafting upon its rules of law with respect to carriage a rule which says that the ship shall not be taken to be guaranteed to be absolutely seaworthy. The word "absolute" means of course just what it says. There was a condition that willy nilly the ship had to be in an implied seaworthy condition. Now you say there is no condition that a ship shall be absolutely seaworthy. I have a good enough opinion of my fellow countrymen and of all others who sail the great waters of the lakes to think that this is a dangerous thing.
It does not say absolutely seaworthy.

The undertaking was implied and it now is no longer absolute. The undertaking is a condition attaching to the contract. It is an implied condition, but there is no longer an absolute undertaking as to seaworthiness.

Would the leader of the
opposition (Mr. Bennett) explain the difference between an implied undertaking and an absolute undertaking? If I sign a note, that is an undertaking, and I cannot plead in court that it is not an absolute undertaking.

That is just the point I am endeavouring to make; that is just the difficulty to which I was referring when I brought the matter to the minister's attention. Certain rules are attached to the bill as a schedule and become part of the bill. Article I of these rules refers to what is a contract. There are questions in these rules which entirely change the existing law with respect to delivery as distinct from merely putting the cargo out on a wharf or a dock. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) asks me to explain the difference between an absolute undertaking and an undertaking. That is used purely in a legal sense. I speak subject to the views of other members of the profession in the chamber, but this is the explanation I would give: When you say that an implied condition attaches to a contract and that it is of an absolute character, you mean that the undertaking is subject to no possible qualification, but when you say it is not absolute, that means it may be qualified. The extent to which it may be qualified under these rules depends upon the considerations which we will speak of when we come to the rules. That is the distinction between an undertaking and an absolute undertaking. An absolute undertaking is an

Carnage of Goods by Water
unqualified undertaking and means the assurance, as the hon. member said, that it is true. On the other hand, a mere undertaking may be subject to qualifications, if it is not expressed to be absolute.
But this section does not relieve the ship owner of all responsibility.

Oh, no.
Mr. HOWE-: I think perhaps I can give an example. The laws require that a ship carrying bulk wheat must have shifting boards. For twenty-five years boats have been carrying bulk grain on the great lakes without shifting boards. A particular type of boat had been built for this purpose and in theory it was thought that shifting boards were not needed. In the Sarniadoc case the boat did not have shifting boards, and this was discovered from a chance remark of the captain that he had not done certain things because he was afraid his cargo would shift. Under this bill such a defence could not be offered.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-Documents of title subject to the rules.

Mr. Chairman, I feel it is my duty to call attention to this section, which has caused a great deal of friction between shipper and carrier. In order properly to understand the section one must turn to article III of the schedule attached to the bill. Section 4 reads:
Every bill of lading, or similar document of title issued in Canada which contains or is evidence of any contract to which the rules apply shall contain an express statement that it is to have effect subject to the provisions of the rules as applied by this act.
In paragraph 3 of article III we find one of the rules referred to in this section. I want to draw attention to this rule because I believe it is not fair to the shipper. It will be noted that this rule first refers to the receiving of the goods by the carrier, and it then goes on to indicate certain conditions. I invite the attention of the committee to the proviso at the bottom of the rule, and I ask hon. members to bear in mind that all these things apply after the goods have been received by the shipper. This proviso reads:
Provided that no carrier, master or agent of the carrier, shall be bound to state or show in the bill of lading any marks, number, quantity, or weight which he has reasonable ground for suspecting not accurately to represent the goods actually received or which he has had no reasonable means of checking.
A shipment of goods consisting of miscellaneous packages may be delivered on a wharf and accepted by the carrier. These packages
are marked in a certain way, which marks are shown on the bill of lading. The carrier, having accepted the goods, may then be asked to issue a bill of lading, which is usually done. After all this has been done, the carrier can then plead that he has reasonable doubts as to the accuracy of the marking of the goods. The marking of goods is sometimes quite complicated, especially when they are being shipped to foreign destinations, but under this rule the carrier can plead, and I believe it is done, that he does not think the goods are accurately marked, and the shipper is out of luck. I know this thing is very often the subject of dispute between shipper and carrier.
While I am quite willing to admit that the carriers should be given every reasonable protection, I do submit that this is a carriers' bill and not a shippers' or merchants' bill. This bill is modelled on the British act which has been notoriously a carriers' act. I am extremely doubtful as to the protection given to our Canadian shipper-that is all we are concerned about-as against the carriers. It will be noted that paragraph 4 of this rule reads:
Such a bill of lading shall be prima facie evidence of the receipt by the carrier of the goods as therein described in accordance with paragraph 3(a), (b), and (c).
If any dispute or difficulty arises the carrier is able to plead that he has reasonable grounds for suspecting that the goods were not properly marked. This whole rule shows how well protected the carriers are. Paragraph 5 reads:
The shipper shall be deemed to have guaranteed to the carrier the accuracy at the time of shipment of the marks, number, quantity, and weight, as furnished by him, and the shipper shall indemnify the carrier against all loss, damages, and expenses arising or resulting from inaccuracies in such particulars.
There is the other side of the story. You are not only imposing upon the shipper the obligation to be accurate in every particular regarding the marks, number, quantity, weight and so on, but you are laying upon him the penalty that if he makes an error of any kind he shall indemnify the carrier, notwithstanding that the carrier has checked the goods, received and accepted them. The point I am arguing is this. When the goods are brought to the ship's side and offered by the shipper for carriage, it is the duty of the owner of the ship or of his agents to check these goods and see that they are in proper form and in accordance with the documents. I am not suggesting that the shipper should be relieved of obligation, but I am protesting, and I know it has been a fruitful cause of

Carriage oj Goods by Water
dispute in years gone by, against the absolute indemnifying of the carrier against loss, and the protection of the carrier if there is any reasonable doubt, whereas the shipper seems to be lost sight of entirely.
I confess that had I known this was coming up to-day there is a great deal of documentation with respect to past disputes that might have been brought to the fore and cited. The subject has not been before me for two or three years and my memory is therefore rather hazy on these technical points; but I do recall some very trying cases that shippers have been confronted with, even under the old Canadian act, which was less drastic than this bill as regards the protection it afforded carriers. While I have a great admiration for British legislation, generally speaking, I cannot help realizing that the chief industry in Great Britain is the carriage of goods by water. The shipping interests there are overwhelming in their influence upon legislation -in Great Britain. That however is not so in Canada, and I question very much whether this country would have gone as far as Great Britain did in connection with the water carriage of goods act. In saying that, I do not wish for a moment to suggest that we should not give adequate protection to carriers, but I think the Canadian parliament is largely on the opposite side of this question to the British parliament. The British parliament would naturally go a long way to protect British shipping, which predominates throughout the world, whereas we are shippers of goods. We are the owners of goods rather than the owners of ships. Consequently if the Canadian parliament wishes to take every precaution to protect the shipper of goods, we cannot expect an act modelled on the British act to provide these adequate safeguards. As I have pointed out, this particular section and the article in the rules based upon this section, would appear to me to be unreasonable in the extent of the protection or the immunity granted to the carriers.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
My hon. friend stresses
England. I may remind him that twenty-four maritime nations have agreed to uniformity in this type of legislation. I was looking at the United States act, passed two months ago, after that country had watched the operations of the English act, and I find that in this respect it is exactly the same as the English act, and the same as this bill. The three contain identically the same clause. If Britain is a nation of carriers, I would point out to my hon. friend that in the United States, as in Canada, the shipment of goods predominates.
(Mr. Stevens.]

The information offered
by the minister is scarcely an answer to the point I have raised. As a matter of fact I differ from him, because in recent years the United States has been trying to rival Great Britain in the carriage of goods. It has made vast strides in'that direction and it might well be that with the enormous amounts of money spent by the American government in building freighters and passenger ships, and with the enormous subsidies they have been granting shipping on the Atlantic and the Pacific, and in fact throughout the world, the American congress may have been influenced in this respect. I am not very much impressed by the statement that the Americans have adopted this precise clause. I was not aware of that fact; I knew they had been considering these matters but I was not aware that they had adopted this precise provision. In any case, it would not be an answer to the question I have raised as to the wisdom of going quite as far as we have gone. The minister has referred to the clause. I should like to know whether the rules in the United States are exactly the same as the rules here, because the rule is what governs the clause, or at any rate it governs the action that may be taken based upon the clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The rules in both countries
are identical. This is rather a large subject to debate, but it does not seem reasonable to me, if the carrier is given a package by the shipper and is not able to verify the contents and weight, that the responsibility should be his. The responsibility with regard to contents and weight should be on the shipper if the carrier delivers the package on the other side.

That is not what we are talking about; that is not the clause nor is it the rule. It is after he has received the goods, after he has had an opportunity to check them and measure them-it is all a matter of measurement-it is, after all, this that we are talking about. The clause which the minister is now referring to is another clause altogether. I believe it is section 7 or section 6 where, if there is a weight which is agreed to by a third party such as an elevator shipping wheat, the carrier has no responsibility for verifying the weight. Here however we are faced with something entirely different. I am sorry the minister does not seem inclined to make an explanation or to throw some light on the subject. I can only say that in my opinion this is .not giving adequate consideration to the rights of shippers. That is all I have to say.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I should be glad to elaborate, but we are passing this act for the sake of uniformity, having complied with the findings of the Brussels convention. It does not seem to me that we can change it.
.Has a convention been entered into? I am not aware of any convention that obliges us to accept the British law in its entirety.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
We were not one of the
twenty-four nations that agreed to it, but since then through correspondence with Great Britain and the United States, I am informed, we have committed ourselves to this bill. The United States passed their act on the understanding that we would fall in line. I do not know whether that is a legal commitment or not.

Section agreed to.
Sections 5 and 6 agreed to.
On section 7-Liability of owner of vessel.

Might it not be desirable, instead of numbering the sections, to obviate the necessity of subsequently passing a statute to overcome difficulties regarding changes that may be made in the numbering of sections in other parts of the act? This, as a matter of fact, is the Merchant Shipping Act, what now we call the Canada Shipping Act, which is being amended at this very session; and we had a similar case in connection with the insurance act. Might we not say, "Nothing in this act shall affect the operation of the Canada Shipping Act limiting liability of the owner of vessels as therein provided," rather than attempt to number the sections? I suggest that because of the difficulty we had with the insurance act; I am not urging it at all. Section agreed to.
Sections 8 and 9 agreed to.
Shall the schedule carry?

The schedule should be taken up carefully, because, as far as we are concerned, it is really the whole of this act. It was the schedule that was discussed. The schedule represents the convention-that is the real fact of the matter-and the legislation is merely to give effect to the provisions of the rules. Since the minister began his explanation I have recalled something of the circumstances to which he refers. An effort was made by the maritime powers to get a
universal 'bill of lading, one that would be adopted by all the maritime countries. It was found that Norwegians were large merchant shippers, the Germans before the war had an enormous amount of eastern shipping, the British also, and others; but we were not there, for a reason which I suppose is quite apparent-that we now have practically no shipping on the high seas. Our shipping is largely inland. It is a long time since the Brussels convention was held. It took place in what year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals

speechtext:
They succeeded in
formulating this set of rules, and that is the real convention; the rest is legislation based on the rules, to give effect to them. There are three things to keep in mind as far as we are concerned. The charter of the ship is altogether a matter of contract between the owner of the ship and the shipper. We have nothing to do, as far as this bill is concerned, with the charter of the ship. But when it comes to the question of the contract for the carriage of the goods, and which by long custom we have called a bill of lading,-just what it says, the bill of what is laden into the ship-under our law both the shipper and the carrier have the right to tally what goes into the ship. The shipper delivers the goods within reach of the ship's tackle, and the ship keeps a tallyman or tallymen for the purpose of ascertaining what goes into the hold of the vessel. The point to which the hon. member for Kootenay East directed attention is one that has been the subject matter of much discussion. When I was a student at law I had cases in which the shipper signed his bill of lading under protest, and he drew up a formal notarial protest in which he claimed he had the right to protest against its being ?aid there were so many standards of deals in the ship when as a matter of fact, according to his contention, there were not that number-or whatever the case might be. He therefore signed his bill of lading under protest and made his notarial protest. Now this is an endeavour to give effect to that rule of maritime law that the master, representing the owners of the ship, signs his bill of lading under protest, but the form whereby it is to be done is a very strange one, and I wondered at the language as it was being read:
Provided that no carrier, master or agent of the carrier shall be bound to state or show in the bill of lading any marks, number, quantity, or weight which he has reasonable ground for suspecting not accurately to represent the goods actually received or which ha has had no reasonable means of checking.

Carriage of Goods by Water
Another paragraph of the rules gives effect to the old common law rule that the owner of the ship checks or tallies what goes into the vessel. The captain is usually the man to do this, or he has one of his officers doing it. It seems strange to say that in lieu of the old form of signing his bill of lading under notarial protest he is to decline to sign that bill of lading by stating-going so far as to say, if he has reasonable ground for "suspecting"-it does not accurately represent the goods actually received. "Suspecting" is a strange word to use in a statute with respect to a contract. When the minister says this represents the rule that has been agreed upon, I suppose it is desirable that ninety-five per cent of the carrying business of the world should be subject to some general rule. We however are more concerned in shipping the goods by freight, by vessel, than we are in the position of the owner of the ship. In other words, we are shippers, not carriers. The United States did not pass this bill, I believe, until two years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Two months ago.

Oh. That explains something that I could not quite understand. If that happened only two months ago I quite appreciate the position, because the United States had declined up to a quite recent time to complete any arrangement by passing the legislation affected by this rule of Brussels. If they have done it now, I suppose it is because the carriers are becoming more important than the shippers, and they are able to influence congressional action, whereas in years gone by they certainly were not. At any rate, this being so, I quite understand the minister's position.
There is one thing I think he might do. It seems to me that in a country like this we should not bind ourselves to this three-day rule. We might modify at least that rule without affecting the general principle. There is no reason why the question of time should not be regulated by the necessities of each country rather than by any general rule. I refer to number six:
Unless notice of loss or damage and the general nature of such loss or damage be given in writing to the carrier or his agent at the port of discharge before or at the time of the removal of the goods into the custody of the person entitled to delivery thereof under the contract of carriage, or, if the loss or damage be not apparent, within three days, such removal shall be prima facie evidence of the delivery by the carrier of the goods as described in the bill of lading.
As the law stood, at least under the ordinary rule governing sale of goods under contract, it was that a man had a reasonable time

within which to inspect and reject or accept. The old rule in our Sale of Goods Act was "a reasonable time." Our old rule used to make delivery absolute. As it is now it is somewhat changed. The carrier hands the goods over, and when they are removed if within three days he does not get notice that there has been loss or damage, the claim to loss or damage is gone. There are certain types of goods, both coming into this country and departing from it, in respect of which it seems to me that three days may be too short a time in which to make it clear that the damage, although not apparent, is there. "Such removal shall be prima facie evidence of the delivery by the carrier of the goods as described in the bill of lading." In other words, he has complied with the bill of lading and delivered the goods safely under the conditions mentioned in the rule, unless within three days the person receiving them gives notice that there are. now apparent conditions which make for loss or damage of the goods that he is receiving.
Why should it be any different in Canada?

Consider our position. First of all we have great frosts and the other difficulties that are incident to climatic conditions, so that what might be apparent in four days might not be apparent in three days with respect to the condition of goods. I do not think there is any point in regard to the arbitrary fixing of the period, but it appeared to me that three days was rather a short time. I recall a case which one always recalls in these matters, of a cargo of turkeys that went from eastern Canada to the west.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They move the other way now.

Yes; the last five years brought that about. The carload was inspected and it was found that it had not been properly refrigerated so that apparently there was a loss. It was contended that the inspection and rejection had not taken place promptly and therefore the owner brought an action to recover the purchase price-at least the bank, as the holder of the bill of lading, brought the action, which failed. It struck me that the officers of the department would be able to tell the minister whether in a country such as this, where we have sudden extreme heat and cold and where we move cargoes so rapidly, this length of time was sufficient. For instance, suppose a cargo was accepted in Vancouver for shipment to Calgary and it made the journey in three days. When it arrived there, as soon as the consignee had an opportunity it was inspected and found to

Carriage oj Goods by Water
be not in good condition, attributable entirely to the voyage. In such a case one might say that three days might be too short a time.
I have no settled views on the matter, except that it struck me in that way. The whole series of rules, as I said in the beginning and as has been said by the hon. member for Kootenay East, is predicated upon the carrier receiving every consideration and the shipper being more or less at his mercy, subject of course to the terms of the rules. Probably it is better to have those rules in that form, so that they are uniform throughout the shipping world, than to rely upon the varying decisions that might be given if there were no uniformity. Every country has its own common law rules. We have rules in this country that are far more favourable to the shipper than these. The statute we are repealing is far more favourable to the shipper than the one we are now passing; it affords him a measure of protection which we do not now afford him. I have no doubt, as the minister has said, that the carriers are pleased to have this statute become part of the laws of this country, but I am afraid that the shipper is less vocal than the carrier because he is not organized, whereas the carrier is organized and speaks with authority and with a single voice when he attends a conference. The only surprise I felt was when the minister said the United States had passed a statute accepting these rules, because I knew that up to a few months ago they had not done so. Then when the minister told me it was only two months ago that this had been done, it removed the necessity for any further observations on my part. With our small shipping I think we were content to become a party to the general convention provided that in addition to the other countries the United States, our near neighbour, accepted it, and that had not been done when I was last familiar with the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: As to the time limit, as I have said this is an attempt at uniformity, but as far as I can see there is no objection to a longer period, if my right hon. friend cares to move an amendment.

I was just asking if the minister had thought about it, because it struck me that three days might be a little too short a time. After all, in a country like this five days might not be too short or too long, but I am not definitely committed to anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Three days is the uniform period.
Then I would hesitate to change it.

I suppose I am only showing my ignorance in asking this question, but perhaps I can obtain some information. I revert to the section referred to by the right hon. leader of the opposition, the proviso at the end of paragraph 3 of article III of the schedule, which reads:
Provided that no carrier ... shall be bound to state or show in the bill of lading any marks, number, quantity, or weight which he has reasonable ground for suspecting not accurately to represent the goods actually received ...
As the right hon. leader of the opposition has stated, this certainly seems to me to be a carriers' bill. Supposing I ship fifty gallons of whisky in a number of demijohns and the man says he suspects that my statement as to the quantity is incorrect. Does he only put down on the bill of lading "whisky"? In that case, when it reaches the other end and my consignee takes delivery, he is entirely at the mercy of the carrier. The carrier may have drunk half the whisky, and then he could say, "All we undertake to deliver was whisky, and you have received whisky." Surely there should be some provision for protecting the shipper; surely the carrier should say "so many demijohns said to contain so many gallons of whisky" or something like that. Apparently, if I am reading this aright, all he has to put down in that case is the article shipped; he is not bound to put down the number, quantity or weight. Would the minister explain that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I think it was explained by the right hon. leader of the opposition that it has always been possible to take a notarial statement casting doubt on the representations made as to the shipment. This is a similar provision. In other words, if you said there was whisky and the other man had some doubt about the quantity, if you still insisted that he take it for delivery I think perhaps he would say on the bill of lading "fifty demijohns full of liquid" or something like that. In other words, he has a right to refuse to put on the bill of lading something he does not believe is true, and I suppose you have your right to withdraw the shipment under those circumstances. I think that is the position.

Then would the minister explain this other point in regard to the definition of goods, contained in paragraph (c) of the definition:
"Goods" includes goods, wares, merchandise, and articles of every kind whatsoever, except live animals and cargo which by the nature of carriage is stated as being carried on deck and is so carried.

Carriage of Goods by Water
Why is that exception made? Within the last two or three years we passed an act by which large quantities of lumber might be carried on deck, so why should that lumber be exempt from the presumed benefits of this act? Since it is not defined as goods I assume it does not come under the act.
Lumber does come under this act but it did not come under the old act.

This definition states:
... except live animals and cargo which by the contract of carriage is stated as being carried on deck and is so carried.
If it is carried on deck it does not count as goods.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That is true. Lumber did not count as goods even if stored below deck under the previous carriage of goods act. Under this act it qualifies as goods if it is properly stowed, but if it is put on deck it is subject to special risks and does not come under the ordinary ship cargo insurance.

Mr. Chairman, from the very nature of it this legislation is intended for the future. The idea has been expressed that the act is extremely in favour of the carrier, and the hon. member for Kootenay East in particular said that we are not a carrying nation but a shipping nation, and therefore-
I did not say that; I said we were not a carrying nation in the sense that Great Britain is.

I quite accept what the hon. gentleman says, but it only emphasizes my point: I hope we do not accept the idea that we shall always be a shipping nation and not a carrying nation. We in the maritime provinces have some aspirations in regard to preserving to Canada the carrying of our goods upon the sea. It is our ambition that in the future we should become more of a carrying nation.

The explanatory note
opposite article III reads:
It will be noted that the carrier is bound to exercise due diligence before and at the beginning of the voyage. The present Canadian statute (section 4) requires due diligence to be used to make and keep the ship seaworthy. It is not practical to require the owner to keep the vessel seaworthy and the wording of the British Act is desirable.
To one who is not particularly versed in shipping it seems an extraordinary statement that the ship owner is not required to keep the ship seaworthy.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
While we will all agree that it is possible to make a ship seaworthy it may not be always possible to keep it seaworthy. In other words a ship may be technically unseaworthy as the result of a storm. It may be made seaworthy again after that, but I think the distinction there may be recognized.
I have a few amendments, chiefly typographical errors. On page 4, section 6, the word "damage" is misspelled, and an "a" should be inserted.
I do not think that is necessary
We do not need an amendment for that.

I move:
That section 6 of article III be amended by substituting the word "damage" for "dmage" in the second line thereof.
Amendment agreed to.

I move:
That	subparagraph	(b)	of section	2	of

Amendment agreed to.

I move:
That	subparagraph	(q)	of section	2	of
article IV be amended by substituting the word "and" for the word "or" in the first line thereof.
Amendment agreed to.

That article V be amended by inserting the words "and liabilities" after the word "responsibilities" in the third line thereof.

That sounds rather strange to me, to provide that a person shall surrender his liabilities. I should think they would be glad to surrender their liabilities at any time. Is that in accordance with the British act?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes. It was left out in the printing by mistake.

It is not a surrender of
