Customs Act

Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of National Revenue) moved the second reading of Bill No. 67, to amend the Customs Act (Canadian waters).
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston (Lake Centre) in the chair.
On section 1-"Officer."

Would the minister be
good enough to make a brief statement as to the general purpose of the bill?

It is a short bill, five sections in all. It is designed to strengthen the preventive work of the customs service. Section 1 defines "officer" as used in the Customs Act. Section 2 defines "Canadian waters" and "Canadian customs waters." Both these terms are new as far as I know. "Canadian waters," roughly speaking, comprise all the marine league, that is the waters included within the three mile limit, and "Canadian customs waters" the waters in the nine mile belt outside the three mile limit.

Why did they make
it that rather than twelve miles?

We would have to have
some description. In the act being amended we referred to them as territorial waters of Canada, or some phrase which I do not just remember, which did apply to waters within the twelve mile limit. But His Majesty's government in Great Britain made representations that it was of some importance not to define territorial waters of Canada in that way. The powers to be exercised outside the marine league, outside of Canadian waters, so-called, are very limited powers.
Police powers, practically.

Police powers, yes. Section 3 provides that certain vessels must carry manifests. Section 4 defines hovering, sets out the powers in respect of hovering vessels and contains other provisions relating to hovering. Section 5 repeals section 207 of the act. I hope that the brief explanation is sufficient for the purposes of the member for Kootenay East.

I assume this bill is for the purpose of the better enforcement of the Customs Act, that it concerns only Canadian shipping, and that the authority is over every Canadian ship within the twelve mile limit.
That is scarcely correct. If the hon. gentleman will look at the bill he will find that vessels other than Canadian vessels are affected by its provisions.
For police purposes only.

For police purposes only. This bill affects vessels registered in Canada and unregistered vessels owned by a person resident or domiciled in Canada and other vessels or classes of vessels specified or enumerated by proclamation of the governor in council. This third class of vessels would be vessels registered in countries other than Canada. But the bill does not assert jurisdiction over these vessels within the nine mile limit unless they are enumerated or specified by proclamation of the governor in council. It is anticipated that that will be dealt with by agreement. For instance Newfoundland vessels in the nine mile belt, outside the three-mile limit, will in all probability be specified or enumerated by proclamation of the governor in council as a class of vessels to which this act will apply.
By agreement.
By agreement between the government of Canada and the government of Newfoundland, and agreements of this nature will undoubtedly be made with many countries.
Have you now an agreement with Great Britain?
No.

The point that occurs to me is that vessels sailing out of Canada might change their registry to Barbados or Bermuda or the Jersey Islands. The Jersey Islands in the past have been a favourite place to register vessels. They have some peculiar sort of independence from Great Britain, and in days gone by to register a vessel in the Jersey Islands gave them almost absolute freedom. Now if this bill is enacted into law, will it cause a certain class of vessel to register in foreign countries and thus give them greater freedom than they would have if they were registered in Canada, although they may be owned in Canada only by mortgage or on shares?

The control over vessels registered in foreign countries which is to be exerted in the nine mile belt outside of the marine league will be effective only if an agreement is made between this country and the country of registry of the vessels. Does that answer the question?
Customs Act
I understand that perfectly. But the point I want to make is that after all this is a very ineffective way of controlling the customs situation. It will' not get you very far, will it?
I do not know why it should not. Canada will have complete jurisdiction over vessels in the three mile limit.
It always had.

And will have the right of pursuit, which is dealt with in the bill. It will also have control over vessels registered in certain countries which make agreements with Canada when those vessels are outside the three mile limit.

Will it not induce Canadian vessels to register in a foreign country that does not have an agreement with Great Britain in order to smuggle goods within the nine mile area without restraint by Canadian officers?

I think what the government has in mind is bringing vessels of a notorious character engaged in certain well known activities within the police powers of this act. If a proclamation were made following an agreement between this country and the country whose ships notoriously engage in illicit operations, such vessels would be subject to the punitive powers we have provided by our statute. Is not that correct?
That is correctly stated.
But the notorious vessels will take care not to register in countries with which you have an agreement.
We believe no country will refuse to make an agreement.

Section agreed to.
On section 2

"Canadian waters."

Since the bill was prepared it has been deemed advisable to strike out the words "and shall conform with," in lines twenty-eight and twenty-nine, so that it will read:
Canadian waters shall not extend beyond the limits of exclusion recommended in the North Atlantic Fisheries Award,
And so on. That makes a difference in the meaning of the section, of course, but it really does not injure the section because in another part it is provided that a map or chart may be issued under the authority of and approved by the governor in council which shall be conclusive evidence of the due deter-

mination of such base lines, and Canadian waters shall not be defined on that map to extend beyond the limits of exclusion recommended in the North Atlantic fisheries award. There is a real reason for the subsection.

I think the addition of the extract from the award as a part of the bill is highly to be commended. It gives to those who read the bill immediate knowledge regarding a matter of some importance, namely, what the decision of the arbitrators was. It gives the information at once by looking at the statute, which I think is exceedingly desirable having regard to the technical character of the answer given to question V as set forth in the schedule.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I move the amendment accordingly, Mr. Chairman.
Amendment agreed to.

I would have worded the paragraph a little differently and said "beyond the limits of exclusion recommended in the answer to question V," but I do not desire to suggest that my draft would be any better than that of the gentleman who drew this.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 3-Master shall have manifest on board.
There is not much difference here except that this makes it obligatory. But most ships do carry manifests that give these particulars, as I understand it.
Many ships carrying smuggled liquor do not carry manifests.
I realize that, but the manifest usually contains this information.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-Application of section.

The minister said that
there was no arrangement with Great Britain. I am puzzled about this because I believe that any good effect to be derived from this bill will be derived by arrangement with other countries. Otherwise, it will only drive ships from our shores until we do have such arrangements. England entered into a twelve mile arrangement with the United States, to which agreement we are a party. Would that not mean that at the present moment we have an arrangement with Great Britain as to the twelve mile limit?

At the present time we
have limited rights over vessels within the nine mile belt, but this section will give us

Supply-Interior-Parks
the right to conclude arrangements with other countries by which we can exercise much more complete control than we can at the present time.

It will be recalled that the United States legislation called for an hour's sail from shore. England and the United States entered into an agreement to this effect; they were the primary signatories, but we were a party. A vessel might register at Bermuda or some other British possession and thus be exempt from the twelve mile limit regulations.

That arrangement does not
enable seizures to be made within twelve miles of Canada. It deals only with seizures within twelve miles of the American coast.
It was a one way agreement.

The minister will remember the circumstances. The Americans were imposing upon British ships a certain condition, namely, that they should not have in their possession any intoxicating liquors while in the United States during prohibition. The gr6at steamship companies carrying passengers across the Atlantic were confronted with a serious situation and as a result Great Britain negotiated with the United States. The United States said that they must have the right within twelve miles of their shores to search and exercise police powers over ships flying the British flag. The price paid for that concession was the permission for British vessels to bring their liquors into American ports. Otherwise, it would have been very difficult for them to operate. The matter was all the subject of diplomatic correspondence and discussion before my time, but the counsel of the department could tell the minister the circumstances. The Cunard line took a very active part in this, and finally the British government secured the rights I have indicated, while they conceded the right to have searches made on their ships and police powers exercised within an hour's run or twelve miles from shore, within nine miles of what was known as the territorial three mile limit.

Section agreed to.
Section 5 agreed to.

I was going to suggest to the minister that it might be desirable in the interests of administration to provide that this act shall come into force on a date fixed by proclamation published in the Canada Gazette. If this legislation became effective immediately there would be no opportunity
for the minister to discuss these matters with other countries and it struck me that his purposes might be better served if the act were to go into force on a date fixed by proclamation, in the same way as we did with the bill we just passed. The minister might also provide that this act shall come into force in whole or in part on proclamation. In practice it has been found very useful to proclaim one section when you could not proclaim the whole act. I make this suggestion only in the interests of effective administration.

I think the suggestion of the right hon. gentleman is a valuable one, especially the latter part with reference to the whole or part of the bill coming into force on proclamation. I shall ask my colleague to move such an amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I move that there be added a new section 6 as follows:
This act in whole or in part shall come into force on a date or dates to be fixed by proclamation of the governor in council published in the Canada Gazette.
Amendment agreed to.
I would direct the attention of the minister to an apparent misprint in the last word of rule 1 on page 7. This word should no doubt be "miles."
That is correct'; it should be "miles."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No motion is needed to correct that.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of the Interior) :
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is not a great deal I can add to the information I gave when the matter was under consideration on the last occasion. We have under negotiation now with the British Columbia government the question of an agreement definitely fixing the completion of what is known as the west leg of the Big Bend highway. It may be recalled by hon. members who were present when the item was last discussed that the arrangement to complete that portion of the trans-Canada highway was embodied in telegrams and letters which had been exchanged. We hope to reach an arrangement with the British Columbia government whereby we shall complete that part of the work within the next three or four years.
As long as that?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly three years, with the understanding that the British Columbia government will take over the maintenance of each year's portion as it is completed. There have been some discussions with that government with respect to the road from Kingsgate into the park, and I hope we shall be able to conclude with them, by formal agreement, an arrangement whereby they will bear fifty per cent of the cost of dust-proofing that road, the federal government to put up the other fifty per cent.
Has that road from Kingsgate been standardized?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not all of it. Part of it is now so constructed.
What distance is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
About 150 miles, from
Kingsgate to the park.
I know that; but how much has been standardized?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: About twenty-four miles has been hard-surfaced, and about a third of the road is graded to standard. I have also had under discussion with the Alberta government the matter of assisting with what they describe as the blotter type of road. I believe that they constructed some mileage of that in Alberta between Waterton park and Calgary. If the arrangement is carried out it will probably involve a total expenditure of $75,000 on the part of the federal government by way of assistance. When that work is completed we shall have the circle from Waterton park right on to Calgary, Banff and Kingsgate, or the other way round, which will be dust-proof, and I believe it will be useful in attracting tourist traffic from the United States.
What part of the park would the Kingsgate road strike?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Kootenay national park, at Radium Hot Springs. I am not familiar with the geography of the place, but I trust that is the information my right hon. friend wants.
What view will the minister take of the suggestion made a year or two ago that a strip of land on the west leg of the Big Bend highway should be created a park?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I was not aware that
such a suggestion had been made, but at the moment I do not see what particular bearing it would have. The road is in British Columbia, and after its completion it is the responsibility of British Columbia to maintain it. I assume they own the land, or the portion that is adjacent to the road. If the hon. member has in mind some particular reason why such a strip should be set aside, I am certainly not aware of any such suggestion.

I am not presently
advocating it, but the suggestion certainly was made, I think in 1934. I heard it discussed. I hold certain views with regard to it which it is not necessary for me to express now if the minister is not contemplating carrying it out.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This is the first I have
heard of it, but my deputy informs me that in 1934 there was some discussion on the basis of the federal government's completing the road and probably maintaining it in consideration of getting this particular strip to which the hon. member refers. What practical value a strip of land on either side of the road would be to the federal government I am not at the moment in a position to say.

I think the information the minister has given is that which the committee was asking for the other day, but I am disappointed to hear him say that it will take three or four years to complete the road to the coast because that will stand in the way of complete means of transport being afforded from the park to Vancouver. There is the old road, and I fancy that cars sometimes go through, though I doubt it. I thought, however, that the road would be completed in less than three years. I say that for this reason. The province of British Columbia entered into a contract to complete the road within a shorter period than that. That is the old contract under which we did some work up to a

certain point, and they were to finish it. I am not sure of the exact date when it was to be finished. This is 1936 and it would probably be 1939 or 1940. Can the minister tell me the date of completion as given in the original contract?

We now hope it will be
finished in the fall of 1939.

Yes. It will now be
193^40, which is a serious matter. If the road from Kingsgate is completed to Radium Hot Springs and made dust-proof, and the same with the road from Waterton park to Calgary, then there has been a certain amount of dust-proofing done between Calgary and Banff; the only other stretch would be from Waterton park to the United States boundary, and that has been put into fairly good shape. Therefore I think it is an admirable enterprise, provided an arrangement is made that will not create a precedent which will be embarrassing to the minister. As to the extent of the contribution, that does not make so much difference, because we must recognize that the road itself as far as the park, between Kingsgate and the park, is the property of the province of British Columbia, and not ours, and therefore we must not put ourselves in entire possession of provincial roads which belong to the crown in another relation, as the minister said the other day.
On another occasion I mentioned to the minister the matter of the completion of the road from Edmonton to Jasper along the line of the old Canadian Northern grade. The minister will recall that the city of Edmonton took up with the then president of the Canadian National the question of the acquisition for highway purposes of the abandoned right of way between west of Edmonton and Jasper park. The president was willing that this right of way should be acquired, but there were certain difficulties- very great difficulties, legally-from the standpoint of securing a good title or a lease for any great length of time. Finally the province expressed willingness to take the right of way and make the necessary changes and alterations to fit it for a highway. So far as I know that work has not been completed, and I suggest to the minister that it would be very helpful if something of the sort could be done, because otherwise it will continue to

be difficult to get into Jasper from Edmonton. The present condition has interfered seriously with the movement of tourist traffic. If the road to Jasper is finished, and then the work upon the line from Jasper to Banff is completed, within a reasonable time there will be a fairly complete tourist highway, meeting the situation, if not as fully as one would like, at least in a moderate way having regard to our financial and other conditions.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I appreciate the importance of the point raised by the right hon. leader of the opposition. This arrangement with the British Columbia government regarding the Kingsgate-Kootenay park road will, if it is completed, constitute a definite agreement covering only that work, and for a specific purpose, also with the obligation upon the British Columbia government to maintain the road in that condition. And it is a relief undertaking.

speechtext: And, of course, it is for the relief of unemployment. Oh, yes, by the board of trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: -by the board of trade of Edmonton. Of course, in all these matters it is largely a question of money. I should like to finish the west leg of the Big Bend highway next summer, if that could be done. But when I bring these estimates, amounting to a good many hundreds of thousands of dollars, before a Finance minister who is rather stony-hearted when it comes to expenditures, I have to take that circumstance into account. If our revenues improve and the situation becomes brighter financially the road might be completed in a shorter period, but at the moment I should not care to give any undertaking that it will be completed before the time I have already mentioned.

I mentioned the Jasper
matter because it is one singularly within the jurisdiction of the federal government, having regard to the fact that the rails and ties have been removed from that section of the right of way west of Edmonton into Jasper, and I think a good deal could be done without

Supply-Interior-Parks

too great an expenditure. This would certainly be helpful in getting into that park, because the road from Calgary to Edmonton is not too bad for motoring, and some steps have been taken to relieve it of the dust nuisance.

Just what work is to be
done this year on the Big Bend highway? We are very much interested in that, because it is the last gap in the western portion of the trans-Canada highway.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think I gave that information before. It is intended to spend about $400,000 on the west leg and $70,000 on the east leg, which expenditure, it is estimated, will complete the latter portion of the highway, including the bridge across the Columbia river.

How much mileage will
remain to be completed on the west leg?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am informed that there
are about seventy-two miles on the west leg yet to be completed, but that portion is expensive to construct. For instance, we had some slides on a portion of the work which has already been done this spring, and it was estimated that it would take a steam shovel two weeks to clear these mud slides off the road. I mention that merely to give an indication of the difficult nature of the country through which the road is being built. However I hope it will be completed within three years.

Does the minister mean that it will take three or four years to complete those seventy-nine miles of road, including the work that is to be done this year? This is important also to the prairie people, because it is their way of getting out to British Columbia, as well as our way of getting to the prairies.

I know the matter has been brought to the attention of the department by public bodies and by myself, but I wonder whether the minister has considered the advisability of establishing a beach park in British Columbia? He has four parks in that province. They are all highly mountainous, with wild and rugged scenery, wild animals, big precipices, hairpin turns, and things like that; but to round off his program I suggest, and others have suggested, that he needs a park on a beach to which people could come, not only from California and the southern states, but from our own country. As times improve we get a considerable tourist trade from the prairies, and I know, from people whom I have met, that very many persons are ordered to leave the prairies and come to the coast, temporarily or permanently, to get

away from the high altitude; it gets on their nerves, and causes a condition which medical men can explain better than I can. If those people can go to the coast for only a couple of months in the summer, spend their time at sea level, with a beach for the kiddies to play on, and enjoy themselves in a quiet way, without any great expense, this would be a tremendous advantage to persons in that condition who have a little money to spend. In my district-and though I am apparently speaking selfishly, I have no personal interest in the matter-there is an area which can be obtained for a mere trifle, having almost every advantage that can be named: a beautiful white beach with no stones on it, warmed by reason of the shallowness of the water and so made suitable for bathing, a beautiful park behind it, close to the public highway, with facilities for electric light almost on the ground, and with trout fishing in the neighbourhood which will provide recreation for adults. I believe it would be a good thing to round out the department's policy by acquiring such a park, and I should like the minister to promise at least to give the suggestion his consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
With respect to the matter mentioned by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill), he has made representations to our parks branch for the establishment of a park of the kind to which he has referred. Any area for a park, of course, must be supplied by the provincial government. Under the act the federal government does not purchase or acquire such property; that is acquired and turned over by the provincial government to the federal government for park purposes. That would naturally be a prerequisite in this case. Then, again, there is the question of the amount of money that the federal government can spend year by year in park development all over the country. I think I mentioned to the committee previously-and, if not, I will do so now-that the total investment in parks in Canada is approximately $30,000,000.
With regard to the other point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South, the matter is not so much one of distance. The seventy-two miles would seem to be a comparatively short distance in order to complete the west leg, but the real question is the amount of money involved. It is estimated that it will cost $2,000,000 to construct that portion of the highway.
That includes the $400,000 being voted this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, of course. If next year I can get a million and a half dollars to spend on that road I will spend that much money,

Supply-Interior-Parks
but it must be borne in mind that certain expenditures have to be made in all these parks. There are roads leading into them; there are in the parks works that are partly completed, and it would be difficult to take the whole vote and spend it in one locality. The hon. member will appreciate the difficulties of a minister who would endeavour to do that. So I am afraid I shall have to ask him to be as patient as possible in connection with this matter, and we will complete the highway as soon as it is reasonably possible to do so.

It may be that the burden is being placed on the wrong department. After all, this question goes much deeper than the national parks. This is one very sure and effective way of drawing the provinces of Canada closer together, and on that ground alone I think the government should see to it that the trans-Canada highway is completed without delay. Perhaps the expense should not be borne by the national parks branch, but certainly some department should see to it that this section of seventy-nine miles of road is completed right away.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The expense is not borne by the national parks branch, but that branch has the responsibility of building the road, so, of course, it gets the money to do the work. As far as the tourist business is concerned I might say that I understand the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have arranged a sort of land ferry for transporting cars across the base of the triangle formed by the big bend of the Columbia river, and it is possible for tourists to leave Vancouver, come as far as possible by road, load their cars onto the facilities provided by the Canadian Pacific and be transported to the road on the other side of the big bend.
Of course the tragedy of that situation is that tourists will not travel that way. They will go by road through the United States, and Canada will lose that business.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We shall get it after a while.

I quite realize that any park taken over by the dominion government would have to be offered to them free of charge. What I wanted, rather, was an indication from the minister that he would favourably regard such an offer and that he appreciated the value of having a beach park. The minister has spoken for quite a while this afternoon as to the various developments being carried on in connection with the interior parks; he has been throwing around sums like 12739-2061
S75,000	as if they were mere bagatelles. There is a public road right into this particular park of which I speak, so the cost of developing the park would be practically nil. The electric line is within a few hundred feet, and nature has done everything else. All that needs to be done in connection with the park portion is to leave it alone, for the most part; it would require only a very small sum, perhaps two or three thousand dollars, to put up a number of cabins such as are common for the use of tourists, and even these could be made self-sustaining by the imposition of a small charge.
With regard to the accessibility of this park, a man and a woman with a car coming from the prairies, however poor their car might be, can cross on the ferry from Vancouver to Nanaimo for a dollar or two, and reach this park in three hours. They do not have to spend two or three days going down through the United States or over impossible roads to get to this park, and then face the necessity of retracing their steps to get home again. This park is thoroughly accessible and would be used to a great extent not only by people from the United States but also by our prairie people and by the residents of Victoria and Vancouver. It would be used particularly by people of the prairies who have to get to this low altitude from time to time because of their health. I meet many people who have come to the coast because they have been told by their doctors that they had to get to a lower altitude because of heart or nerve trouble. The cost would be absolutely a bagatelle. If the minister will give the offer favourable consideration I will guarantee to do the rest. We will deliver the park to him on a platter, and the expense of developing it would be practically nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am always glad to give consideration to any suggestion that may be made by my hon. friend. I have just had handed to me a brief memorandum, in which the point is raised that the area of this proposed park, which is 321 acres, might not be sufficient for a national park. Probably that matter could be adjusted if we were in a financial position to allow us to go ahead with it. That would depend upon financial conditions which at the moment we cannot foresee. We do not know what our revenue is going to be for the coming year. If it increases, as we hope it will, it may be possible to extend our parks operations. If conditions are such that we have to limit the expenditure of money, then I am sure my hon. friend will appreciate the significance of that fact.
Supply-Interior-Parks

The area is small, but in a case of this kind it is quality we want rather than quantity. This particular park has a beach which I think is about a mile in length. A picnic was held there last year which was attended by five or six thousand people, and the beach could easily have held three times as many. There is no danger of its not being ample for the ordinary traffic that might be anticipated for quite a number of years to come.

It has been interesting to ' listen to the remarks of the minister in regard to these parks throughout Canada, especially the statement that 830,000,000 has been invested in the national parks in the different provinces. I was also interested to hear the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill), with three or four parks in British Columbia already, asking for another. The other evening we were discussing a park in New Brunswick, and at that time the minister stated that the creation of a park in that province depended upon factors as to which I should not care to pass an opinion at the moment. I should like to ask the minister just what really are the factors which are holding up the creation of a park in New Brunswick. I was pleased to note a vole of
8100,000	for a park in Nova Scotia. It is pleasing to know that the members from Nova Scotia have been able to sink any differences of opinion that they may have had, and to decide on a site for a park. The same is true of Prince Edward Island, but the people of New Brunswick would like to know what is holding up the development of a park in that province. If the minister can give me that information I shall be glad.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think what I stated when the matter was before the committee previously was that a definite area had not yet been selected for park purposes in New Brunswick. An investigation was made by one of the officers of the parks branch, who examined several sites. I believe he recommended one particular site, but considerable objection was taken to that by certain interests within the province which did not think it suitable. When a site for a park is once determined, it is fixed for all time to come, and consequently I am sure the hon. member is impressed with the importance of having the selection wisely made. It is better to make haste slowly and make the best selection, rather than act hurriedly and get a location which perhaps for all time after one would regret. That is why no selection has been made definitely in New Brunswick.

Then, of course, there is another fact. The government of New Brunswick will have to deed over free this park area, so naturally the government of that province is interested. We hope to get further with the matter this year; we shall have further reports, and if circumstances warrant it we shall bring forward a recommendation next year for the establishment of a park in New Brunswick.
I thank the minister for his explanation, and I would like to ask if in Nova Scotia the provincial government has already deeded over the site.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The area has been selected in Nova Scotia. The Nova Scotia government had to acquire certain private lands, but they advise us that they expect to be able to turn over title of that park area to us within a short time, probably during the coming week.

For a long time I have been interested in conservation work. I see one item in this estimate, namely, forest and game conservation works. I have been working for the past two days in connection with conservation for Ontario-
Of the party!

-assisting in selecting the
new premier-to-be of Ontario, when the provincial government next goes to the country, so if the minister has answered any questions in regard to this item I can look up in Hansard what he has said. If he has not, I shall be glad to have some explanation of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think it was referred to when the matter was under consideration be-1 fore. This item is to provide for telephone lines in some of the parks, and the making of trails and roads to facilitate the park wardens in getting over their territory and making contact with their central authorities as rapidly as possible. Some of these park areas, particularly at Banff and at Jasper, are very large. We are making every effort to conserve the game and the beauty of the parks. In the judgment of those responsible for the administration of the parks these amounts are necessary, and those responsible carry my judgment with them in that respect.

With respect to this particular matter I desire to make some observations, which I will make when the bill in respect to the Nova Scotia park is before the committee. I find it a little difficult to accommodate myself to the view that one should be called and the other not. I suppose the minister thinks he is following the

Supply-Interior-Forests
words of Scripture, "the one shall be taken, and the other left." Just why New Brunswick should be left and Nova Scotia taken I find it difficult to understand, except that when I look around on the Nova Scotia members,
I realize that they are more insistent as supporters of the administration than are my New Brunswick colleagues in their attitude towards this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I assure the right hon. leader of the opposition that he is quite mistaken. Of course I did not find any opposition to this park among hon. members from Nova Scotia. I have not the necessary information definitely to reach a judgment as to the best location in that province; that will have to be determined this summer. As I stated a moment ago, if our financial circumstances warrant-and I think perhaps they will-there will be provision for a park in New Brunswick next year.

All these stations, with

Supply-Mines
To assist in provision of transportation facilities into mining areas, $1,500,000.
Can the minister give some particulars?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The purpose of this vote is, as stated, to assist in the provision of transportation facilities into mining areas. Within the last five years there has been a notable extension of prospecting, exploration work, and the development of new mines. In that period, for instance, mines have developed in the Great Bear lake area, away up on the rim of the arctic circle, where they are producing silver and radium. I believe there are three small mines operating in that area. Transportation costs amount to $140 a ton from the end of the railway at Waterways in northern Alberta. In the Central Patricia area there are two mines operating over 100 miles from the railway, producing gold to a value of approximately $250,000 a month. My information is that their freight costs from the railway line to their mines are about sixty dollars per ton. Instances of a similar kind could be multiplied, although perhaps not to the extent of the same cost as far as other mines are concerned. The purpose of this vote is to help reduce, where possible, those costs. It is also intended to use a part of it in opening up new areas. For instance, in British Columbia, north of Prince George, there is an area known as Manson Creek. Quite obviously it is out of the question to build a railroad into that area, but we propose to assist in the construction of a motor truck road to it that will enable the people who are operating there to bring in their supplies and to do their business more economically, from the point of view of freight costs, than they are doing at present. I expect that, as a result of this, there will be a stimulation of development in many areas of Canada.
We have not as yet quite determined how the vote will be divided so far as the provinces are concerned. I have discussed the matter with representatives from all the metal mining provinces and suggested to them that the provinces should put up one-third and ourselves two-thirds; that is, for every two dollars we put up the provinces put up one dollar; and they have agreed, without exception, to that suggestion. In the result there will be available altogether, between what the provinces supply and what the federal government is providing under this vote, something over two million dollars. In selecting the areas that will be assisted we have consulted with the provinces. We do not propose to spend any of this money in
[Mr. Crerar.l
building roads to a prospect where some person thinks he has a mine; there must be reasonably evidence that there may be a mine there. In many cases we know the mines are there, because they are producing, and as far as one can judge now, some have a promising future. Approximately it will probably work out in this way, that British Columbia will get about $300,000 of this fund; Alberta, a comparatively small amount, because there is as yet no metal mining in that province, but there is some work to be done.
How much?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I said, a comparatively small amount. As yet there is so far as I know, no metal mining in Alberta. But the waterways into the great northern hinterland, pass through the northern part of Alberta to this area at lake Athabaska, where a mill is being established; to Great Slave lake, where drilling operations are going on, and then to the region up in the Great Bear lake area. Freight for each of these points is moving to Waterways at the end of the steel in Alberta, and by water transportation from there on. In many cases there are portages which are extensive, where freight has to be unloaded, and reloaded again after the portage is crossed. An examination is being made to see what assistance can be given there with a view of reducing the cost of transportation. That principle will apply all the way through. Manitoba will probably get between $260,000 and $270,000; Ontario, probably $325,000 to $400,000, and a somewhat smaller amount for Quebec. Roughly, that is the classification of this vote. I wish to make it clear to the committee that so far these arrangements are only tentative; they are not completed. I think the vote will be of considerable assistance. I hope a little later, when we come to our main estimates, to give the committee some information as to the development which has taken place in mining in Canada during recent years.

No item in the estimates has caused more unfavourable discussion than this, for reasons that I think the minister must easily appreciate. In the first place, except in the Northwest Territories, any work done on a highway to improve transportation, means work done upon roads entirely under the control of the provinces. No federal money can be expended by the federal government on a provincial highway or transportation road or colonization road without the consent and approval of the provincial authorities. The principle that is to govern should not be unlike that which governed an appropriation of several million dollars for the construction of roads many years ago. That money was divided among the provinces on the basis of population. It will be recalled that at that time the senate insisted that this should be done, and on the part of the then Liberal opposition there was a great deal of discussion and, frankly, some opposition to the proposal to utilize federal money for the purpose of improving highways in provinces. That opposition was overcome by the method I have indicated, namely a division of the money on the basis of population. A standard type of road was agreed upon, and the work was done under the inspection and, shall we say, the general supervision of the late Mr. Campbell, who represented the federal power.
This is an appropriation of $1,500,000 to be expended on the improvement of transportation to mining claims in every part of Canada. There are still some mining claims left in Nova Scotia, for instance, in connection with some minerals other than coal that are being sought for there. The disaster about which we were all so much concerned recently had to do with an old gold mine that was being exploited. In New Brunswick there are still some mining claims left, though comparatively few. In Quebec there are the great northern areas where the general formation is similar to that of northern Ontario, and it is proposed to divert the same sum
Supply-Mines

of money to each province for the improvement of transportation.
When I asked what principle was to govern, the minister said that the money would not be spent to improve transportation to what a man might think was a mine. But if geology is a science, as it is, and if the reports of those who have made surveys of the territory are worth attention, it should not be a case of what a man thinks. I had concluded that the minister would say that this money would be used to enable promising areas to be prospected, because if the mines have come into production they do not require much assistance in the construction of roads. By reason of the fact that mines are producing, they have ample money with which to provide transportation to the markets for their products; they have ample money with which to carry on their operations. That is not the case, however, with a great area which has been, shall I say, closely investigated by geologists in the manner in which that is done nowadays, and which is very interesting even to read about. When an area is regarded by geologists as being promising then it is of first importance to get diamond drills and other necessary equipment into that area, and in that case some expenditure is required to be made to enable transportation to be carried on.
From what has been said by the minister I gather that this is not what is intended. I repeat that a mine already in production does not require very much assistance. If it is producing even' two or three days a block of gold worth $25,000, $30,000 or more, it does not require much help in order to provide transportation. I thought the minister was going to say that this money would be spent in order to encourage the development of the mineral areas. Certainly the amount of $1,000,000 which was appropriated by parliament last year to enable investigations to be undertaken had behind it the idea that we would become familiar with geological conditions and the extent to which work might be carried on in given areas for the purpose of securing valuable metals through the development that was to go forward. Until the minister spoke I had certainly concluded that this, in a sense, was to be supplementary to what was done last year, so that areas of promise would be made possible of development by reason of these expenditures, in cooperation with the provinces, to enable the transportation of supplies to be carried on. The hon. member for Renfrew South spoke of aeroplanes being used for the transportation of supplies. In the Northwest Territories,

which are completely under the jurisdiction of this government, every dollar of this sum could be spent and still it would not meet the requirements, so difficult is transportation into that area.
The minister knows that we have spent a considerable sum of money in providing radio stations for the purpose of enabling news to be sent into and out of those areas, and although it has been very expensive we have endeavoured to do something in the Great Bear lake and Slave lake regions. Both of those mineral areas are in the Northwest Territories, if I am correctly informed, and I would think it desirable that as much money as possible should be spent there, where we have no province with which to cooperate or consult, where we own the highways and everything else. It occurred to me that the minister might say that a good deal of this money would be spent there, where any revenues, royalties or fees come to us and not to any province. We have supreme and complete control over that area, which contains pitchblende, copper and some promises of gold. I do not know that the gold deposits have been developed to any considerable extent, but certainly other minerals have been reported there. I was surprised at the small sum the minister mentioned as having in mind to be expended in the Northwest Territories. If he will look at Hansard to-morrow he will see that it would appear that this money is to be used on behalf of those who least require it and not in aid of those who most need it, and when I say that I mean those who as yet have not been able to demonstrate that a given area will be productive, those in territories that geology, which is a fairly exact science, has indicated might contain gold-bearing rock or quartz. It is in such territories that one would expect at least a good share of this money to be expended in order to make transportation feasible.
I have nothing to say with respect to the situation in Alberta. There is very little in the way of mineral deposits in southern Alberta, though, of course, in that province they have the fields where they have been prospecting for oil, -which is almost as important as minerals from the standpoint of the immediate production of new wealth, and I suppose these petroleum products might, in a sense, foe classed as mineral wealth. In the northern part of the province, however, bordering on the Northwest Territories, as the minister has said the waterways require some attention. I had hoped that in connection with those great Northwest Territories, where

Supply-Mines
last year considerable geological work was done and where every promise was found of rich deposits of valuable minerals, the minister would say there is a duty devolving upon us, for we are both the province and the dominion as far as those territories are concerned. Wherever there is a possibility-and I do not want to use that word in too narrow a sense-or, we shall say, a geological probability of there being valuable mineral deposits, as far as we can we should use this money for the purpose of making it possible to have those deposits developed.
It would seem to me to be a very great mistake to leave entirely in the hands of the provinces the selection of those on whose behalf and for whose benefit this money should be expended. On the other hand, of course, we cannot expend any money in this way without the consent of the provinces; that is obvious, and therefore there must be cooperation between the provinces and the dominion. The extent to which that cooperation will be given will depend entirely, it seems to me, upon the view the provinces may take as to the desirability of this or that area being assisted in the way of transportation facilities. If an agreement cannot be reached, then I suggest that the money should be expended where I expected the minister would spend most of it, namely in the area where there is no province, no government except our own, nobody to receive any benefit except the people of Canada who derive the whole benefit, both in respect of any income the companies may secure and in royalties that may become payable on the minerals taken out. I cannot say that I congratulate the minister upon the method he proposes to adopt, because I cannot help thinking it will bring him a good deal of difficulty, and in' the end the money will be frittered away without any corresponding advantage.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think my right hon. friend need not have the fears that he has just expressed.

I have heard a good deal
about this vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have, too, heard a great deal that is favourable.
I have heard a great deal that is favourable for one or two people.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As far as the Northwest Territories are concerned, to get back to the Great Slave lake and Great Bear lake region, practically all the expenditure that has to be made in order to give transportation into those areas has to be made in Alberta.
You cross the boundary line and get to where you leave the river, and then you have to get to where the claims are located. On Great Bear lake you go by water.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: For instance, on Great Slave lake, which is wholly in the territories, the mining claims that have been prospected and explored are on the north shore.

speechtext: They get to lake Athabaska by the river from Fort McMurray. One of the chief difficulties of transportation into that north country is the stretch of river for six miles north of Fort McMurray. In low water the boats cannot get up to rail head. We do not propose to undertake any work this year by way of deepening the river.
Is there not a small item in the main estimates for that?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There may be for investigation, but deepening the river would involve blasting rock out of the river bed. The solution of the problem is probably either a motor road for six miles from Fort McMurray to a point where the boats can take their freight-
Or an extension of the railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Or an extension of the railway.
Both expensive.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is partly within the Northwest Territories one other portage on which some work will be done, and indeed some has been done. To-day a private company has the privilege of carrying freight over that portage.
They get how many cents a pound?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They get a good rate; I have forgotten what it is.
It is a very large figure.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Of course this is in the north country.
To come to another point, the assistance is not alone for mines that are developed. It may be a nice question to what extent a company producing, say gold, should pay the expense of providing the highway or railway to the mine. For instance, there are at present two mines working in the Central Patricia area. The likelihood is that within twelve months another mine will start operations;
Supply-M tries

that is, steps will be taken to get in mill machinery and the equipment and accessories necessary for the successful operation of a mine. If the first mine there builds the road in, the second mine is at the mercy of the first. Consequently the highway should be in the nature of a public highway.
The province has control of that though.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Quite so. I fancy, however, that if the mine which commenced operations had the responsibility placed upon it of building the road, at a cost of, say, $100,000, it would not undertake that work unless it had some way of collecting tolls from others using the road. This brings up the question of the regulation of those tolls. That is largely a new principle in the development of the country. We are applying here a principle which has always been applied.
Is it not a very old one? Long before confederation they had toll roads.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This work will be done
in conjunction with the provinces under agreements. My right hon. friend when he was Prime Minister made agreements with several of the provinces for work on roads. That was done, for instance, in Manitoba in 1936; there were definite agreements covering the work. That did not commit the federal government to the principle of building roads in Manitoba.

No; those were existing
highways.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In some cases they were
not
All of them were, I think.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No. There were one or
two cases where a road might be called a highway, but it was only a rough wagon road.
Does the minister mean the one in the park?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The one in the park and
the one from Dauphin to Winnipegosis. The point I am making is that my right hon. friend adopted that principle. What we are doing is precisely the same thing. We go to the province and make an agreement in respect to a mining road, after we have mutually decided where one should be built. The province bears one-third of the cost; we bear two-thirds; they agree to maintain the road and to bear all the expense of engineering and supervision. That is to be

covered by the agreement just the same as the Russell-Clear lake road in Manitoba a year ago, or the one from Dauphin to Winnipegosis.

Or the road running
south.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes.	We are following
under this vote precisely the same principle and the same practice as were followed then. Now the advisability, the wisdom of this expenditure might be questioned. Personally I think it will be money well spent. The increase in mineral production in recent years has been phenomenal. I shall give some figures on that when I come to the main estimates. What is expected from this vote, and what I think will certainly ensue, is a stimulation and aid to the development and production of a great deal of real wealth. That is the purpose. The problem of the expenditure of the money will be studied, is being studied with the provincial departments of mines. They canot say, as my right hon. friend hinted, where this money will be spent; that has to be agreed upon between the two governments. We shall use our best judgment in deciding where the expenditure will produce the best results. As far as the vote itself is concerned I have had a good deal of commendation for this step having been taken, and so far no criticism. The only criticism that I anticipated is that the vote is not nearly large enough. There are a great many cases where the people think they need assistance; many of them do need it, but broadly speaking what we propose to do is to spend the money so that in the years to come we shall get the greatest possible results from it.

I am bound to say
that my hon. friend the minister did not quite follow me. I am certainly fully aware of all the agreements made between provinces and the dominion, and I was not in any sense taking exception to the good example given by the late government being followed by the present administration, in this as in many other things. What I was endeavouring to direct attention to is that the principle adopted in determining what mines should receive the benefit of the vote is a principle with which I could hardly agree, because it does not touch what I conceive to be the general idea underlying the policy of the government in making this grant, namely, to secure further development, and the creation of more new wealth. I was suggesting that that result be brought about by utilizing the geological surveys and determining with the cooperation of the provinces

Supply-Mines
what areas would likely be benefited by development; that is, where it would be probable that suitable returns and probably a mine would result from the efforts which might be made in that territory. I thought the money would be used in such areas rather than where established mines already exist. On the other hand, if this is merely for assisting the provinces to provide transportation to known mines, then, of course, it is nothing more or less than the application of the general principle that has been applied during the last three or four years with respect to such highways as the minister mentioned, such as there are, for instance, in Saskatchewan extending west, and in Alberta and other parts of the western provinces. My anxiety was to ascertain the general principle that was to govern. I was approaching the matter from the standpoint of the money being utilized to assist in the development of new areas and the production of new work rather than for the purpose of providing better transportation facilities in areas where it had already been demonstrated that satisfactory results had followed the efforts which had been made to establish mines. The latter view, of course, can be supported, but I had assumed the other view, that a province being unable to undertake an exploratory road, the dominion had said:	We
realize that any new wealth you develop will be to our benefit as well as to yours, and we shall therefore assist you in territory that our department and your own geologists believe to be promising. But, as I say, the view which the minister has put forward can be supported on the general principle that, wealth having been discovered, it is the duty of the state to endeavour to make it available. That is the general principle you would be following if you are going to use the money in territories already developed.

The minister made no reference to any amount being set aside for Nova Scotia or the maritime provinces generally, and I was wondering whether it was his opinion that they did not need any assistance. In the county of Antigonish-Guysborough which I represent there has been considerable gold mining activity recently, and I have no doubt many companies there would be glad of assistance. The government that was in power in Ottawa started in 1928 and 1929 to build the Guysborough railway, which would have been of considerable assistance to the people there, but in 1931 the government under the present leader of the opposition did not see fit to continue the construction of that road. I would ask the minister if Nova Scotia and the maritime provinces generally will receive consideration under this vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Some consideration has
been given to that question, but transportation costs to the mines in Nova Scotia to-day are relatively low, whereas in British Columbia, for example, there are mining areas that are from fifty to seventy-five or even one hundred miles away from a railway and are without roads, yet they are producing placer gold and have indicated that they can develop others. Obviously it is at just such points that assistance is needed rather than where transportation costs are at present relatively low. The same argument would apply to New Brunswick, where I understand there are no metal mines. I hope that one day there will be a revival of the gold mining industry in Nova Scotia. Without doubt the increase in the price of gold has helped the gold mining industry of that province. On the other hand, many of the mines to which I have referred to-night are large potential producers situated in favourable areas. I might mention again the Central Patricia region which affords a splendid illustration. Two mines there are now producing approximately one-quarter of a million dollars worth of gold a month, and it is costing them $60 a ton to get their freight in. Should either of those mines have a major break in its equipment it would be tied up for six months unless the replacements could be carried in by aeroplane. Conditions of that sort we are seeking to overcome, and if we could get a road into that region or assist in cheapening transportation costs into it, the likelihood is that within the next twelve or eighteen months there might be three or four more mines in that area. It is with the idea of stimulating such developments as rapidly as possible that this vote is placed before the committee.

What about a mine that is a paying proposition? Does the government build a road into an area where there is a paying mine, or does the mine or the province put up a certain portion of the costs, or just what arrangement is made in building a road under those conditions? Is it built under the plan of two-thirds of the cost being met by the dominion government and one-third by the province, or do the mines themselves that are paying producers pay any portion of the cost of building the road?
