speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is not contemplated that the mines would pay any portion of the cost, because such mines have spent a great deal of money in providing present transportation facilities. I have in mind, for instance, a mine north of Port Arthur producing chromium ore. They nave to transport that ore twenty-five miles to the railway. That mine supplies a great deal of freight to the Canadian National Railways every year, and the industry is still only in its infancy. Probably we shall provide
S5,000	or $10,000 to help gravel their road.

Item agreed to.
Mines branch-for investigations of mineral resources and deposits; of the mining and metallurgical industries, and of mineral technology; wages, and expenses of testing and research laboratories; for publications, English and French; for purchase of books and instruments; for miscellaneous assistance and contingencies; and for investigations by the Dominion fuel board, including salaries and all other expenses, $250,000.
Mr. CRERAR; I think it might be interesting to the committee if I gave a survey- and I shall make it as brief as possible-of some of the facts that indicate the value of the mining industry to this country. It is interesting in an historical sense to note that the first suggestion for making a geological survey was made in Upper Canada about one hundred years ago, in 1836, and the motion asking that a small amount of money be appropriated for that survey was moved by a gentleman who afterwards acquired a great deal of publicity, William Lyon Mackenzie. In the political troubles which followed, prosecution of the work was lost sight of until after the union of Upper and Lower Canada, and then in 1841, as a result of suggestions made by the National Historical Society of Montreal and the Historical Society of Quebec, a resolution was passed appropriating £1,500 for the purpose of causing a geological survey to be made of the province of Canada. The expenditure of this money was entrusted to William Logan, who later became Sir William Logan, and who was for some years the head of the geological survey. Later on, in 1855, a further appropriation of $20,000 annually was made, and $8,000 was set aside for the publication of the results of Logan's explorations. It is an interesting fact to note that his work was so thoroughly done that where he reported favourable geological formations in areas in Ontario and Quebec our great metal mining development has since taken place.
Mr. BENNETT; And in British Columbia too, later on.
(Mr. Donnelly.]

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That publication was given to the public in 1866, and along with it a geological map was published. However the mining, industry did not attract a great deal of attention in Canada, and it was not until 1907 that the Geology and Mines Act was passed and a definite effort made to bring about development work. The work done by the mines department falls into four divisions. First, there is the geological survey, which covers the sending of survey parties to the field to search for favourable formations. Second, there is the ore dressing and metallurgical plant on the outskirts of the city. Third, there is the division for testing fuels, oils and coals. Fourth, there is the division of ceramics where a study is made in the use of the various clays to be found in Canada.
The work of the ore dressing plant particularly has attracted international attention. When the Ottawa conference was held in 1932 it was attended by the Premier of Southern Rhodesia. Southern Rhodesia has large mining possibilities, but the ores there are of a complex type and prior to that time they had been unsuccessful in discovering a proper method of treatment. As a result of inquiries made here and an examination of the ore dressing division of the mines branch, two tons of ore were shipped to Ottawa and the officers of the division worked out a treatment for the ore. Many of the mines in Canada have testified to the useful assistance given by this division. I mention this merely to indicate to the committee that the mines branch is performing a very useful service for the country.
If the committee would bear with me I should like to give a few figures indicating the growth of the mining industry in Canada. In 1901 the value of the metals produced in Canada was approximately $25,000,000. In 1935 this had grown to over $220,000,000. Of this latter figure, $116,000,000 was gold, $88,000,000 was base metals and the balance was made up of various precious metals, such as silver, platinum and other metals found in small quantities in some of our larger mines. It may be of interest to the committee to know that in January, February and March of this year our gold production exceeded the production of the corresponding months in 1935 by 174 per cent. The total value of all mineral production in Canada in 1935 was $310,000,000.
The contribution made by the mining industry to the railways of Canada is considerable. I was surprised when I noticed a statement by the president of the Canadian:

Supply-M ines
Bank of Commerce in the annual report of that bank to the effect that the mining industry contributed practically one-third of the total freight handled by the Canadian railways in 1935. I had these figures checked and I found they were correct, according to the information in the possession of the bureau of statistics.
That is directly and indirectly.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That includes ores, coal, stone, gravel and everything that is classed as minerals in the records of the bureau. In 1935 the Noranda mine paid over $1,000,000 in freight. Ten years ago there was not one dollar's worth of freight originating in that area. Hudson, which is on the Canadian National Railways on the way to Winnipeg, produced no freight ten years ago, but in 1934 the freight receipts from Hudson totalled $232,000. In 1935 the freight receipts from Ilford on the Hudson Bay railway, 286 miles north of Le Pas, in the distant northern part of Manitoba, totalled $150,000. The freight receipts directly and indirectly from the Flin-Flon mine of the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company in northern Manitoba totalled $1,302,000 in 1935, Consolidated Smelters have contributed in freight payments an average of $4,000,000 per annum during the last ten years.
That would include ore from the Sullivan mine at Trail?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is the total freight contribution of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company.
Is that $4,000,000 per annum?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is the yearly average for the last ten years. The International Nickel Company pay over $1,000,000 per month in wages. The Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company have paid over $76,000,000 in wages in the last ten years. Since 1911 the Hollinger mine has paid over $79,000,000 in wages. In 1935 the mining industry as a whole contributed $88,000,000 in wages.
In connection with supplies we find that in 1934 heavy mining machinery, practically all of Canadian origin, was purchased to the extent of $6,500,000. Purchases of lighter equipment, such as rock drills, pipes and fittings and so on, amounted to $3,250,000.
Did the minister say that was practically all Canadian production?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Practically all of Canadian origin. In fact, practically all mining supplies are of Canadian origin with the exception of certain chemicals which cannot be secured in Canada.
Drills are now being made in Canada as a result of the tariff policy of the late government.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Electrical equipment to
the extent of $2,125,000 was purchased. As an illustration of the value of this industry in another field, the mining region round Sudbury used over 40 million feet of lumber in 1935, and I am told that over eighty per cent of this came from British Columbia. In the way of foodstuffs the mining industry consumed last year 38,000,000 pounds of meats, 7,500,000 pounds of lard; 7,500,000 dozen eggs; 11,000.000 pounds of butter;
7.500.000	pounds of cheese; 760,000 sacks of flour; 114,000,000 pounds of potatoes, or
57.000 tons, and there were	over 100,000 pounds of turkeys shipped from the western provinces into the Porcupine and K-irkland lake area.
I venture to say that very few people in Canada appreciate fully the very great heritage we have in the mineral wealth of the country. It extends practically from Labrador round the south shore of Hudson bay, swinging north to the arctic circle, east of the Mackenzie river; and so far as our geological information goes we may expect to find mineralized areas, some of them rich, over that vast extent of territory. I do not think it is an impossible dream that we can within the next five or ten years increase by fifty or probably seventy-five per cent our metal production in Canada, and I know of nothing that will contribute so much to placing this country in the way of permanent national recovery as the sound development of our mining industry. I apologize for taking up the time of the committee in supplying it with some of these facts, but I thought it might be of interest to hon. members in the consideration of these particular estimates.

I am very much interested in what the minister has said. Most of his remarks were confined to the precious metals, but I should like to say a word in regard to the baser metals, particularly iron. The minister spoke of mineral development either having been recommended or having commenced in Ontario about 1836. The iron industry in Ontario commenced about 1815. I am not sure of the exact date, but I believe the first development took place near
Supply-M ines

the west boundary of the present county of Lanark, though they did not begin to smelt there at that time. The first place in which iron ore was smelted in Ontario was at the ancient village-there is still a cluster of cottages in the locality-of Normandale, founded by one of the early pioneering families, Van Norman, of the province. I have always been interested in the iron industry, and for some time past I have been trying to dig into the early history of iron production in Ontario, which is not known to many people in Ontario, and certainly not to the people at large throughout Canada. It is not generally known that our first real iron industry in Ontario began at Normandale. The ore was what was known as bog ore. During the last couple of years I have covered the district many times and have been intending to get into touch with the Department of Mines to find out whether it is possible that there may still be some ore there, because at one time there was quite a pocket in the county of Norfolk, about seven miles north of the present site of Normandale. Later, after that ore became exhausted in Norfolk, a considerable pocket was found in the adjacent county of Elgin. Two others of our principal old pioneering families of Ontario were associated with this original Norfolk development of the iron industry in the province: a pioneer named Tillson, after whom the present Tillsonburg was named, in the riding of the hon. member for Oxford, and the Leonard family, who were also associated with the Van Normans, later established in London, where their descendants are still making the very good Leonard boilers. It is remarkable that at Normandale in those very early days, about 1820 or 1822 and prior to about 1848, they melted approximately 900 tons of iron a year, which they dug out of the swamps and bogs in that locality, a very fine iron. It was a soft iron and when smelted and poured it had to some extent the texture of what is now known as malleable iron; it would almost bend, and one characteristic was that it did not rust easily. Last summer I went into a wood just north of Normandale where I saw one of the old stoves made in Normandale, bearing the date 1845, and it had been in the farmer's back lot many years and showed no evidence of rust. I wonder if the department has ever made an investigation in that locality to see whether this ore is really extinct. The soil seems to me to be very much like the soil west of Duluth, where there are vast iron ore ranges.

I have often thought, in connection with the development of iron ore in Ontario, that if Ontario ore is suitable-and I am going to speak now of the ore in the vicinity of Sudbury; I believe it is what is called the Atikokan range-and if the government would produce the iron by smelting the ore by means of electricity, seeing that there is ample power there, and then dispose of it to the iron foundries in the province at cost, on the same basis that the hydro electric commission of Ontario delivers power to the factories in the province, the government could not do better to develop the iron industry in the province. Though, as I believe, ore was first smelted in Canada a few miles north of Three Rivers, I do not think there is any doubt that the iron industry in quantity really began in Ontario. If there is iron in the province and it can be economically developed, it would be a considerable boon to the great iron industry of Ontario, which is our basic industry next to agriculture. Agriculture comes first and then iron. At the moment, so far as I remember, no iron is produced in the province, although many long years ago, away back in the 1820's, as I have said, in that little village of Normandale, on the shores of lake Erie, they smelted 900 tons of bog ore a year. I once saw in one of the Toronto newspapers the reproduction of an advertisement that appeared in 1830, indicating that 1,000 stoves had been received from the Normandale foundry. It is interesting to know that so long ago in this province we did smelt iron ore in a village that has passed away. Four hundred men were engaged in fabricating iron in that industry.
I am glad to endorse whatever the minister can do to develop mining. What he has said as regards the development of mines in this country, and their tremendous importance to Canada, is perfectly true, and it is all new money. If there is iron in Ontario, even in those places where it is now supposed to be extinct, and if iron can be produced in this province, the government should do whatever it can to assist in the development of the industry. It would result in a good deal of employment in Ontario factories.

As my hon. friend from Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) has told us something of the families originally settled in Normandale, I should like to inform him and the other members of the committee that the Van Normans came to the city of Brantford and associated themselves with the Watrous family, and the Watrous family established what was known as the Watrous Engine Works and is now known as Watrous Limited. I mention this that the committee

may know that it is Watrous Limited of Brantford which manufactures a great deal of the mining machinery that is not now used in Norfolk, but is used in northern Ontario and all parts of Canada.

This afternoon I asked certain questions of the minister with reference to the number of persons likely to be employed as a result of this vote and other votes of a like kind. Perhaps the minister now has the information and can give it to the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The total number of parties, as worked out to the present time by officers of the department, will be fifty-seven. There will be a total of 392 engaged in the work, or, including the chiefs of parties, 447.

I assume that most of the men who go on these parties will have had some technical training, probably in the universities. In spite of the fact that most of those young men will require a certain amount of training, has the minister had any difficulty in filling these vacancies?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No. I believe I intimated to my hon. friend this afternoon that there had not been any difficulty in filling the vacancies. These parties are staffed in the following way: There is a chief of the party. He has an assistant geologist, depending upon what particular field he is going to work in, and there are student assistants. These latter are selected from the various universities, from students who are taking up geology and mining engineering and are in their second, third or fourth year. They get their ratings through the civil service commission, and as a result of those ratings the commission give us a list from which the selections can be made. Then the selections are made on the ratings supplied by the commission. It is interesting to note, though it is not quite germane to the question my hon. friend has asked, that several of the universities of Canada are recognizing the importance of geological work and some of them are providing excellent courses. That is all to the good as far as this industry is concerned. I may be unduly optimistic, but I am of the opinion that, for the next ten or fifteen years at any rate, mining will be the large developing industry in this country. It is, if I may use the term, one of the coming industries for Canada during the next ten or fifteen years. We have to provide the technical men who are required, and it is a matter of satisfaction that bright young fellows are taking up the study of geology, mining engineering and electrical engineering. I have been told by some of the larger mining companies 12739-207
that they are experiencing some difficulty in getting technically trained men. The expansion of the industry in the last few years has been so rapid that the trained men graduating from the universities have had little difficulty in finding suitable work, and very often remunerative work, in this particular field of endeavour.
(Qu'Appelle): How many of these parties will go into northern Saskatchewan, and how many young men are being accepted from the university of Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There will be seven parties out in Saskatchewan. I am unable to give my hon. friend information as to the latter part of his question, but I am informed that as far as possible students were taken from Saskatchewan university, in some cases students who graduated within the last few years and who are resident in Saskatchewan. So far as possible that method has been followed in staffing these parties.
How many parties will there be in British Columbia, and in what parts of the province?

It will be of interest to the committee to know that so far as Manitoba and British Columbia are concerned, under arrangements made, I think, at the time those provinces came into confederation the federal government has to carry on the geological survey work of those provinces.
That is in the British North America Act.

Can the minister say to
which parts of British Columbia they are going?

The extra vote is to take rare of that expense?

speechtext: Yes, vote No. 153 covers that.

I think the committee
must be under a sense of obligation to the minister for the very frank and interesting statement he has made as to the development of our mining industry. I have read some of the addresses he made over the radio; I heard one of them, and I realize that the industry has become very important. But there are one or two observations I should like to make, not in any critical sense, but rather, I hope, in a way that will be helpful to the minister in dealing with some of the problems which he has to meet.
In the first place I think it highly undesirable that there should be duplication of effort. We have a national research bureau; we also have this research bureau for mines. And it must be remembered that outside the Northwest Territories we have not the remotest interest in these mines except as mining corporations may pay us taxes. There was a time when the crown in the right of the dominion had a direct interest in some of these mineral areas, but outside the Northwest Territories we now have none. One of the problems that every government in this country will have to face is the extent to which the federal power shall maintain facilities that are used by industries over which the provincial power has complete control in the matter of royalties and in the determination of the terms and conditions under which the industry shall be carried on. I found, as undoubtedly the minister has found, that the maintenance of this mines branch and this

research bureau was in effect the maintenance of an organization which received its raw material entirely from outside,-I am eliminating the Northwest Territories for the moment-from provincial sources. When, not by the action of any province but solely because of economic conditions to which this country as a nation contributed, the price of gold went to $35 an ounce, and the suggestion was made that a portion of that increment between $20.67 and $35 should be paid into the national treasury, such a furore of opposition was created from one end of the country to the other on the part of the mining interests that I really thought it was an extremely unfair attitude to take. The nation and not the provinces had brought about the end by means of which these industries profited greatly. For example, they were able to use lower grade ore, that in days gone by they had abandoned, for the production of gold at $35 an ounce instead of $20.67, which was the former statutory value of it, and for which the dominion could continue to purchase gold if it so desired. Yet from their annual meetings they sent statements all over the world complaining to their shareholders that the dominion had taken a portion of this money, although it was a very small portion at that.
That brought to my mind as nothing else did the fact that here we were maintaining a research bureau at very substantial expense to dominion taxpayers; yet when an effort was made to secure a portion of the money that came to this industry by reason of national policies and the general economic structure of the nation a tremendous objection was made. Why, I used to receive letters from shareholders in the United States and other parts of the world complaining of the burden of taxation we imposed upon the gold mining industry of the country. That made me think then, as I now say to the minister: Why should we engage in research work? Why should the nation engage in that work when the matter is purely provincial? The province secures the royalties; the province controls the areas; the province owns the mines, as far as the crown is concerned. It is the crown in the right of the province, not in the right of the dominion.
The second point is that we are maintaining a research bureau of our own. Why should we maintain a second one for a specific particular kind of commodity? That was the second point, to which it was difficult for anyone to furnish an adequate answer. It is not as though our situation were similar to that of South Africa. I do not know whether the minister has had his attention directed to

Supply-M ines
some of the reports of the great mining companies in South Africa, but I saw some a few days ago and put them to one side, intending to bring them here. There is a series of companies operating in the Rand in South Africa, and the taxes they pay to the state are so great that they bear a direct relation to the entire production of gold in that area. The Rand gold is extracted from quartz lying many hundreds, if not thousands, of feet below the surface. They have now completed their investigations, their diamond drill boring and so on, and they know that the Rand is capable of producing gold for a period of many years. Perhaps that gold production will continue well into the second century. That is why the other day South Africa paid off part of its national debt. That is why within a very short time South Africa will become a creditor nation. There has been a general disposition on the part of the proprietors of those mines, in Great Britain and elsewhere in the world, to complain as to the burden of taxation; yet they have paid handsomely and willingly.
I mention this because it has to do with the dominion engaging in research work in connection with this industry when we already have a research council, and in at least one of the provinces similar work is being done, though not to the same extent. I mention this to the minister lest in his enthusiasm for the mines he should forget that vast sums of money have been expended, at times when it was difficult to find money, and that it is no more than right that there should be some contribution back to the state in connection with that which belonged to the state and with which the state parted. The crown was trustee for all the people, and when the crown parted with any precious metal it did so on terms that involved the payment of a royalty of some kind. That always has been the law; that shguld be the law, and I assume it always will be the law. As trustee for all the people, not for a few of them, the crown has to distribute the burden as well as it can over those who are winning great rewards from the utilization of these resources which are vested in the crown as trustee for all the people.
Let me sum up that phase of the question by suggesting to the minister that he should investigate very closely the question of duplication and determine whether it is desirable, with respect to matters over which we have no control, to maintain research bureaux of this kind when we already have a great national research council which might do the work. That means that there is no coordination; that there is lack of effective, direct control over the whole enterprise; it means that one department, instead of making its contribution to 12739-207J
the general research effort of the country, is maintaining its own organization for its own purposes. In the same way we have at Montreal a timber testing laboratory. It would be very difficult to justify that by any principle that could be thought of, since we have brought into being a general national research council.
Now we proceed to the second point to which I desire to direct attention, that is, that the influence which the winning of great mineral rewards has upon the nation as a whole is very subtle. I believe from what I have read that for every dollar which this country has taken out of mines it has probably put back two dollars, or perhaps five dollars; some put it as high as that. If hon. members ever took ithe trouble to think of the various mining stocks which they have owned at some time, I wonder how many have ever received any return from their expenditures? That has been going on all over the country. It is a dangerous thing to suggest that because, in some instances, there has been a certain measure of success, everybody is warranted in paying ten cents a share for the * beautifully engraved certificate which, in the end, sometimes represents little or no value.
I mention this because there are other branches of human endeavour of which we sometimes think too little, which produce very great rewards and much new wealth without the corresponding risk of loss of such vast sums as have been lost in mineral exploration in Canada. I should not care to repeat figures given to me by those who thought they were in a position to speak of the relationship of the expenditure to what we have been able to obtain-I am speaking now of the more precious metals, where the returns are great once you have returns, but where there have been so many failures-but I think the minister should keep that in mind, lest we too strongly emphasize one phase of our national economy.
Let me put this to the minister: What we are endeavouring to get is new wealth. Every new country desires to produce new wealth. The complement of that is that we desire to produce it as quickly as possible. That is the reason why vast sums are spent in endeavouring to find petroleum, because, when found, it brings immediate returns. And of course the same thing happened there; promoters immediately began to offer certificates. I am happy to say that I never did; I sold only one that I bought, though the temptation was very great; so I can speak on that point without any personal feeling. But this is the point; Petroleum, once it is found, brings immediate new wealth. Did hon. members ever
Supply-Mines

think of the amount of time that must elapse from the moment a man kicks a piece of rock, picks it up, looks at it and thinks: There is evidence of a rich vein of gold, until the first gold brick comes from the area? Did hon. members ever think of the amount of money that has to be spent and the time that must elapse? On the other hand, if you happen to strike a pool of oil you get immediate returns.
But there is another side of the question. Take our wheat; wheat has become of tremendous importance in our national economy. Why? Because you sow it in the spring and reap the new wealth in the fall. The reaping of the new wealth in the fall meant that you had available within the period of a few months vast sums of money which represented the return from an effort made only a few months before. That is the distinction we must always keep in mind between the development of gold and mineral areas and the development of purely agricultural areas. Agricultural areas produce the new wealth almost at once; therefore agriculture must be the basic industry of a country such as this. Mineral development will produce new wealth, but sometimes you have to wait a long time for it. Unfortunately, also, it is a wasting asset, for whenever a ton of quartz is taken out of the ground, milled and the gold taken from it, it is so much waste material; it is gone forever, whereas the soil properly cared for by rotation of crops and the addition of fertilizer may continue to produce prolific crops for centuries. Those are the distinctions which I suggest the minister must keep in mind, because the change in the price of gold from S20 to $35 an ounce was a sudden one, and we are dependent upon that new price of gold for this abnormal development. There would never have been this enormous development but for the fact that what was formerly low grade ore has now become profitable. I mention this in order to suggest to the minister that we must never forget to maintain a proper balance. For instance, in an English journal the other day I read an article in which they quoted from the Minister of Mines, indicating that he thought the day of agriculture in Canada is about ended.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I never said that.

Of course the minister did not mean any such thing. I heard what he said and I saw it in print afterwards, but that is the construction that has been placed upon it, which indicates the absolute necessity of not putting too much emphasis upon any

one particular industry in our economy. I say that the production of new wealth from mines and minerals has in the main been fraught with great uncertainty and the expenditure of vast sums of money and that the returns have very often been greatly delayed from the time the initial effort has been made. What kept this country solvent for twenty-five years is the fact that in that other branch of our national endeavour we had immediate returns of new wealth from the effort made during each year. Perhaps no one knows that better than the minister himself.
I mention this fact merely because it is desirable that while we rejoice, as we all do, that our mineral production has increased from $25,000,000 to $222,000,000 in the period from 1901 to 1935-and it is a very great progress- at the same time all one has to do is to read Mr. Vaughan's life of the late Sir William Van Horne to realize that half a century ago when the first train of the Canadian Pacific railway reached Port Moody, no one was thinking that between the lakes and the mountains there was territory capable of producing new wealth to the extent of hundreds of millions of dollars every year. Yet, for over a quarter of a century that territory was producing millions of dollars of new wealth year after year in the very year in which the effort was made. That has had the most significant influence upon our economic life of any single factor in our development, because never have so few people, as far as the ordinary history of the world is concerned, produced so much new wealth in a given time as has been produced within the last thirty years between the lakes and the mountains in this dominion. That, I think, is borne out by the statistics of world production.
I do not in any sense disparage the effort to assist in the development of our mineral resources; neither am I one who believes that because it is a wasting asset we should remember that we owe some obligation to posterity, because if we are right in our view there will be ample left for succeeding generations. But I am not unmindful of the fact that as I travelled over the Cariboo country I had pointed out to me localities where within the lifetime of men who were with me there had been considerable settlements and wealth had been produced by millions of dollars; yet that has all been abandoned, and the old Cariboo trail is but a memory of past greatness. All one has to do is to go to California and look upon the remnants of what was once a great industry there to realize that a wasting asset in our generation is after all, something to be thought

Supply-Mines
of and considered when we are dealing with the question of the production of new wealth, for nothing is worse for the state as such, it has always seemed to me, than the spasmodic production of new wealth. That is the reason why agriculture is, and always will be, the basic industry of the country, and the difficulty with agriculture at the moment is to procure with extended production adequate markets. Even with the drought conditions we have had in the territory west of the lakes, agriculture is still the basic industry of Canada.
I am not saying this in any way of criticism of the minister or of the efforts he is making in developing the mining industry. I am simply observing that in order to maintain a proper balance one must never forget that great as is the mining industry and important as is the production of new wealth from that source, yet the greatest source of the production of new wealth in this country has been, during the twenty-five to thirty years of its greatest expansion, those vast agricultural lands between the lakes and the mountains, and notwithstanding anything that may be said to the contrary it is to agriculture we must look for the stable production of that new wealth which is essential for the continued steady development of this dominion and its economic life. If we undertake, I repeat, the duplication of existing facilities -and we are undertaking them without getting any thanks, getting nothing but complaints at what we secure by way of taxes from those who receive the benefits-I think we might consider the whole situation in the light of the factors which, I believe, are important at least in determining the policies we should pursue with respect to the development of mineral and other areas and industries of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I find myself in agreement with practically all that my right hon. friend has said.
I hope the minister does not think he is wrong because he is in agreement with me.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No; once in a while both
might be right. I certainly agree with what my right hon. friend has said as to the importance of agriculture in the country's economic life. No one who has studied its record can be blind to the fact that that great area in the prairie provinces which has suffered so severely in the last four or five years has in its time, as it will do again, produced a very great deal of new wealth.
Whether the research laboratories of the mines branch should be brought under the national research council is a matter of opinion.
It is.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Certainly the laboratories
were established long before the research council, and established at a time when I believe scarcely a province had a department of mines. Whether they should be maintained separately might be debatable. But in the field of agriculture, the great basic industry of this dominion, the federal government has assumed the responsibility of establishing experimental farms in practically every province.
The constitution by section 94 provides for that.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I was not aware of that.

Oh, yes, my hon. friend
was Minister of Agriculture.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not so familiar with the constitution as is my right hon. friend. At any rate this branch of the Department of Mines has been efficient in its work.
I agree.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Whether or not it should be put under the research council is a matter of opinion. I am informed by my deputy, who is a member of the research council, that the work of the council and of this branch of the Department of Mines is coordinated; there is cooperation between them, doubtless with the objective of getting the best results. So far as economy is concerned, I doubt whether very much would be saved by putting the mines branch under the research council.

If the minister will look at the report of the national research council and then look at the laboratories of the Department of Mines, he will see that there has been duplication. That is all I have to say.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not wish to see duplication that involves the unnecessary expenditure of public money. I appreciate what my right hon. friend has said about my enthusiasm for mines.
That is not a fault.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He was hardly putting it correctly. If he had spoken of my enthusiasm for mining development I would have agreed with him.

We have heard several interesting discourses on mining and we must all be more enlightened than when we came into the house. There has been very little said that was of a controversial nature. There is one question, however, to which I wish to direct the attention of hon.
Supply-Mines

members, and that is with regard to taxation. Personally I cannot see why the mining industry should be singled out for this taxation.
What taxation does the hon. gentleman mean?

I understood the right hon. leader of the opposition to say that ihe had received from the people interested in mining a number of complaints against the taxation which had been directed against mines.

No; against the tax on the difference between the statutory price for gold of S20.67 and $35. We did impose a tax upon the increment between $20.67 and $35, and there was keen criticism and a great deal of objection to it. That was the particular tax I was speaking of. I am sorry if I did not make myself clear.

I was just going to say that we had spent a great deal of money on agriculture, fishing, shipping and a great many other things, and that we had done more research for these other industries than we had done for mining. Apparently I misunderstood my right hon. friend.

Item agreed to.
Mines-salaries, $530,152.75; contingencies,
What changes are there in this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is an increase of two employees in the staff of the mines department, as will be noticed by the details on pages 87 and 88 of the estimates. The extra positions provided for are: one geologist, one assistant geologist, and one editor. Offsetting this, the salary of one stenographer, grade 2, has been dropped. Provisions has to be made for the three new positions as they were recreated early in the fall of 1935 as a consequence of the relaxation of staff control regulations by order in council of July 16, 1933, whereby effect could be given to acting promotions made at earlier dates. The increase of $9,994.57 in the vote is due, first, to the salaries of these three positions and, second, to the statutory increases that apply.

I am not going to deal with this at length because it would not be fair to do so in view of the fact that the government has been responsible for this department for only a few months. I have always been curious-I never got round to getting an adequate answer-as to why we should engage in the museum business without undertaking any real work with respect to the 
national museum. We have a palseobotanist ; we have an invertebrate palaeontologist; we have an archaeologist and we have other "ologists;" we have our editors and our statisticians; I have found that we are endeavouring to maintain in each department a self-contained structure. In view of the union that is about to take place between the Department of Mines and other departments it struck me that this item in its present form was hardly an adequate expression of what it was hoped to do. This department is to be merged with other departments; other considerations will enter into its administration, and I can say now that the former Minister of Mines, Mr. Murphy, along with a group of officials in other departments, prepared a memorandum looking towards the union of this department with other departments and what might be effected in the way of reductions. I cannot say that everybody agreed to the reductions. If the minister will look at the list of 198 people on pages 87 and 88 of the estimates, I think he will have a clear understanding of what I mean.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have looked at it.

I have no doubt the minister has looked at it. I certainly appreciate his feeling in that regard, but I suggest to him that the uniting of this department with other departments offers an admirable opportunity for the minister and his staff to take drastic steps in the way of the reform of what I regard as the tendency, not in this department alone but in all departments, to create a self-contained unit of the public service in each department. It was not easy to break this down and it has not been entirely broken down, but at some time or another it is bound to be. Take, for instance, the creation of assistant deputy ministers. There was about as much necessity for that position in this country as there is for a fifth wheel to a coach. Yet the minute one department had an assistant deputy minister, every other department wanted one. One department was not to be outdone by another and the result is that we have an assistant deputy minister in,
I believe, every department of the public service.
The government can hire but never fire.

The striking evidence during the last few weeks and months is hardly an adequate expression of that fact. I can only say that judging from what I have myself observed during the last few months. Probably the minister will say that they were but copying their predecessors in that regard. Be that as it may, I think there is room for a

of duplication comes up. The Department of National Defence is taking photographs in connection with the development of its air service. So far as I know, the Department of the Interior has not at present any air force for the purpose of taking photographs.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have no air force.

These aerial photographs are being taken by the Department of National Defence for the purpose of affording opportunities to men in training. That was what was intended-to afford opportunities to men in training to get experience in the air, taking photographs of the country over which they pass. But this item apparently is for the purpose of developing the survey work which they have done. As I remember, it was thought that this item would not continue to increase, and though apparently it is not increasing it is still over $100,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I understand that there
is a coordinating committee and all these air surveys and pictures are correlated for the purpose of producing maps. I appreciate
3248	COMMONS
Supply-Interior-Geodetic Survey
fully, I hope, the need of doing away with overlapping in the various government departments. I do not know that blame can be attached anywhere particularly-
I agree.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: -because this condition has simply developed. I was surprised, when I endeavoured to make a brief survey of the numerous branches under my direction, to find that there were duplications. I shall not attempt to suggest why it happened in that particular way. I will say, however, that my earnest effort is going to be directed towards creating an efficient administrative unit, and from my experience in the past I maintain that where you have duplication of expense and duplication of effort you lave not efficiency.

I think that in this case the coordinating committee set up for this purpose has been successful in its survey work and in cutting out duplication. It is all under the direction of that coordinating committee and each of the contributing departments fits into the scheme in accomplishing what the committee arranges.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is largely true.

Item agreed to.
Geodetic Survey of Canada-
Control operations-precise levelling based on mean sea level, triangulation, geodetic astronomy and investigations-all basic for correlation of water areas, power developments, charts and maps and for the scientific study of the earth's crust, curvature, figure and dimensions. The above is the recognized basis of operations for federal and provincial departments, municipal authorities and engineering projects over the whole country, $134,600.
To recoup the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway Commission in connection with their claim for injury to John Hedin, $240-* Total, $134,840.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have a note with respect to geodetic survey, which is a little beyond my knowledge. I will read for the information of the committee this note with regard to the functions of the Geodetic Survey of Canada. They are:
To determine the geographical positions of horizontal control points throughout Canada by means of geodetic triangulation, geodetic traverse, geodetic astronomy and radio observations, all points being based on the North American datum.
If the members of the committee are any wiser after hearing that description of the functions of the geodetic survey-well, I simply congratulate them. What is a little more

intelligible, to me at any rate, is the following:
To establish bench marks throughout Canada by means of precise level observations, whose elevations are based on mean sea level; and by collecting, correlating and adjusting the results of engineering levelling to place all elevations in Canada on the same sea level datum.
I understand that these are the means by which accurate surveys are made. I do not know that I can add anything to that.

Two years ago it was
suggested that a new method of ascertaining these points might be followed with success, at not so great cost, in connection with the actual work. Of course, this necessitates actual travelling over the areas to fix the points, having regard to the conditions that prevail from the standpoint of the magnetic needle and matters of that sort, and higher mathematics must be had recourse to. The exact point is located by triangulation and the fixed stars, and a few factors of that sort, the method being the same by which Columbus steered his course to America. It is a highly complicated application of higher mathematics. A few years ago the matter was brought to the attention of the government and an effort was made to devise a new plan to lessen the expense, in view of modern scientific developments. I do not know how far it got, because at that time it was only in its infancy, and I do not suppose that anything further has been done. This method of geodetic survey has for its object a thoroughly legal and complete description of points in this country. It has been going on now for a very long time, I think little by little for a period of at least twenty-five to thirty years, and it will not be finished for another twenty-five or thirty years, if then. For instance, we have been settling the boundary between the United States and Canada, and as far as I know now there is at least ten years' work in sight before it is concluded. The point I desired to make was whether any success had been achieved in devising a less expensive way of doing the work. At the present time it is very costly.

A few moments ago I asked the minister with regard to making surveys of the inlets and the bays of the Pacific coast of British Columbia. I am not sure whether this matter arises under this item, but I should like the information. What I have particularly to say is-and he can tell me if I am wrong-that I think more attention

Supply-Interior-International Boundary
should be paid to the surveying of the Pacific coast. Hon. members will realize that when I tell them that the Japanese fishermen have better surveys, obtained from their own country, of our Pacific coast than we have in British Columbia. The Japanese fishermen using this coast have up to date maps of our coast. It is just about time we took note that we are very far behind in the making of surveys. Surely we should have modem surveys of our own coast line. It almost makes one hang one's head in shame to see these Japanese in possession of better maps than any that are available to us. I would ask the minister to look into the matter and see that more survey work is done so that our own people can have up to date maps of our bays and inlets going all the way from the United States boundary line to Alaska.

I might point out that that is under the Marine department. Hydrographic surveys have been going on steadily for a period of fifteen or twenty years, but the truth is that in the main we still rely upon the British admiralty charts for much of our, shall I say, authentic information in connection with the bays and inlets and harbours of the country, but we are making some progress. On the Pacific coast it has been slow. I am sorry to say that what the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) has said is true. Another country can give us hydrographic maps of the west coast of British Columbia that are more complete than any we have available. Such as we have are, in the main, those that were completed for us by the British admiralty many years ago. Our own hydrographic work has been very, very slowly done. I think we have now a fairly complete map of Vancouver island and of that area on the west coast which runs from Vancouver harbour north to as far as Powell river, or somewhere in that locality, but beyond that, up towards Prince Rupert, I think there is nothing.
Nothing done at all.

Except there is something in the Queen Charlotte area and up towards Prince Rupert, which was done in a preliminary sort of way when that ship, the name of which is probably known to the hon. member for New Westminster, spent a summer there before confederation in doing hydrographic work. Beyond that I fear little or nothing has been done.

Item agreed to.
International Boundary Commission - expenses connected with the maintenance in a state of effective demarcation of the international boundary, $29,200.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is mainly in connection with the international boundary.
How far is that work done now? I am curious to know.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am told that this is maintenance I understand the vote varies to some extent from year to year.

Yes. But the line near where the Premier mine is situated-Alaska is on the other side-was completed about twelve or fifteen years ago. The line travelling east from British Columbia over the mountain areas and then along the plains has been all marked; I do not know how far this demarcation has been done in the east. I remember looking up the mountain side and seeing the clearing that had marked the boundary line as defined by the surveyors of that time. Of course the line has been there ever since the last arbitration took place in the far west, which was finally settled by the old emperor of Germany, but as I understand it this work takes care of the demarcation of the exact spot and the marking of the lines by proper cairns. The line was down in southern British Columbia, between there and the United States. I just wondered how far it had been completed in the way of permanent markings. I do not know.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I understand it is practically completed. There are a few places, such as my right hon. friend refers to, where matters are still under discussion as between the United States commissioners and the Canadian commissioners.
It is nothing very important.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is so. The main part of the vote, however, is for the maintenance of the monuments that mark the international line.

Item agreed to.
Government of the Northwest Territories-* salaries and expenses connected with the administration of the Northwest Territories Act and ordinances, Northwest Game Act and regulations, Eskimo affairs, Wood Buffalo park, reindeer industry, game preserves and sanctuaries, wolf bounties, exploration, investigation and development of natural resources, fire protection, construction and maintenance of buildings, schools, hospitals and roads, relief to destitute, maintenance and transportation of prisoners and insane patients, equipment and supplies, contingencies, et cetera, $187,700.

I was going to mention the case of Mr. Douglas, the stipendiary magistrate in the Northwest Territories. It was said that he was removed from his position for the purposes of economy. He was appointed some years ago; I think he was in the house when the Minister of the Interior was here; and I noticed in the press that he was removed. I put a question on the order paper, and the reply was that he was removed because the duties had been taken over by somebody in the Department of the Interior, as a matter of economy. What official took over his duties?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Douglas was removed from his position, or rather the position was discontinued and the duties assigned to Mr. Norquay. The two of them were under salary, and the duties discharged by Mr. Douglas, which I think were magisterial duties of a kind in the Northwest Territories-he lived in Edmonton-weTe taken over by Mr. Nor-quay. The reason as given to me is the one that was stated in the answer to the question.
Oh, I have no doubt as to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think the appointment was really under the Department of Justice, but the salary was paid by our department.

I think it might be well to ask the minister a few questions, in order that the public may understand how the administration of the Northwest Territories is carried on. Perhaps the minister would indicate how the Northwest Territories are governed at the present moment through the Department of the Interior, how its ordinances are enacted, how they receive the authority of law, with what subjects they deal, the general scheme of administration in connection with mining recorders, fishing regulations, policing, radio and other matters affecting the well-being of that enormous area. Perhaps the minister would indicate something as to the population, the number of white people who are supposed to be within the area and the number of Indians. It seems to me it would be helpful to have that on record, because nowadays many people are interested in the Northwest Territories, having regard to the mineral development that is taking place there.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know that I can give all the information my right hon. friend has suggested.

Many members of the
house are new, and I thought they would like to know something about that vast area.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am, in a way, new too,
as far as the Northwest Territories are concerned. On the basis of the 1931 census the total population is 9,723, of whom 1,007 were classed as white, 4,046 as Indians and 4,670 as Eskimos. I take it that the Eskimo population is largely an estimate; probably it was not made up by actual count, but at any rate the records available give the population as I have just stated it. The government is carried on by a council under the Minister of the Interior. There is a commissioner, a deputy commissioner and five councillors, appointed by the governor general in council. The commissioner in council has power to make ordinances for the government of the territory under the instructions of the governor general in council or the Minister of the Interior, respecting direct taxation within the territories in order to raise revenue, and so on; the establishment and tenure of territorial offices and the appointment of officials; maintenance of prisons; municipal institutions; licences; solemnization of marriage; property and civil rights; administration of justice and generally all matters of a local nature. That covers a considerable range. Fortunately the population is not very large, so the duties are not very heavy.

It is practically section
92 of the British North America Act applied to the Northwest Territories.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. That is vested in
the federal authority.

Perhaps the minister might
give the committee the total cost of the government of the Northwest Territories.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The vote for this year,
covering the matters mentioned under the item we are discussing, is $187,700, which is a reduction of some 160,000 from last year.

But there are some other
costs which should be added in order to give the total cost of government in the Northwest Territories, are there not?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is all that comes under this department. There are other matters under other departments, such as the maintenance of the police, any public works that might be undertaken, and so on.
The radio.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, the radio which is
under the Marine department, and so on.
Is there a similar system in the Yukon territory?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, to some extent similar.
MA\:

There is no elective
assembly in the Northwest Territories at the moment. Government is carried on by this council of seven members who sit in Ottawa and pass the ordinances ito which reference has been made. Would the minister tell me how many people are receiving salaries in the Northwest Territories and what salaries they receive?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There are twelve in the
head office at Ottawa, and the total salaries *will be S14.364, according to the estimate, after allowing for the deduction of five per cent.
How many in the territories?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am informed that there are two mining inspectors, two clerks and a number of medical officers.

Where are the mining
inspectors now?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: At Fort Smith and Cameron Bay. The medical officers are located at Fort Smith, Aklavik, Chesterfield, Pagnirtung, Resolution, Great Bear Lake, Fort Simpson and Good Hope. The last four are part-time officers.
Are there any other administrative officers? Of course the police come under another item.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. I think the only other senior official we have is the man in charge of the reindeer station.

Does any one of the
seven governors of the Northwest Territories reside there? Either the chairman or the deputy chairman was there at one time. Is he still there?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Cumming is at Fort Smith.

Perhaps the minister
would tell us about the reindeer now.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The herd has been safely
delivered on the east side of the Mackenzie river after a journey from Alaska that occupied the better part of three years. The last report we had in August gave the number in the herd as 2,960.
As of what date?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: At the round-up in August last.

How many left Alaska?
I did know but I have forgotten.
29, 1936	3251
Supply-Interior-Northwest Territories

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: About 3,000 left Alaska, and there were 2,370 delivered. Evidently there was some mortality on the way. I hope this reindeer herd will justify the high expectations that were held in regard to it when the enterprise was undertaken. It is necessary, I am informed, to maintain guards for the reindeer to prevent decimation by wolves and Eskimos. There is an assistant superintendent and several labourers. The total cost is estimated this year as $21,800, covering everything.

I think if the minister
will look he will find that the arrangement is older than three years. I think Mr. Stewart, his predecessor in office, made the arrangement. At one time it was not quite certain whether they were going to be got over at all, but they were finally got over.

Some of them
went back.

Yes; I think that is true; they fled from the wrath to come. They had heard of these Eskimos and Indians and wolves that the minister has been speaking of, and they went back. The $21,000 surely involves more than the mere keep and caring for the reindeer. We have got them safe now on this side of the Mackenzie river and now their fives are threatened by the wolves; we pay a bounty for killing wolves and we also take care of the Eskimo, so the problem is: What is going to happen to the reindeer? Santa Claus will perhaps come down with them.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Well, to ibe perfectly
frank, I know very little about these reindeer.
I believe I am correct in saying that certainly no responsibility can attach to my right hon. friend or his government.
Oh, I was not speaking about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think the intention was
a very good one, and they may serve a very useful purpose. It seems to me that as the years pass the federal government is being pushed further and further into responsibility for looking after the native inhabitants of this country. From my brief experience in the department I imagine I can foresee that the government's responsibility to the Eskimo is likely to increase rather than to decrease.
I think that is sound.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If we can provide them
with means of subsistence I think it is good business, and when I reflect on the fact, which

Supply-Interior-Northwest Territories
I think I mentioned to the committee when the estimates of the Indian Affairs department were before it, that we paid out in relief last year about $900,000 for the care of Indians, I aim to create, if possible, conditions that will prevent the Eskimo from coming on relief. How far the reindeer will help in that direction remains to be seen.

If we do not try to
civilize the Eskimos they will never be on relief.

It is only civilized people
who are on relief.

Can the minister say
whether the reindeer are staying put, or are they wandering?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are herded.
The idea was that they should go into that area and spread, was it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They are under the care
of herdsmen; they travel, I understand, over a considerable area in order to find pasturage. In the autumn they are rounded up into their winter quarters.
No; we set aside an area for them.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They are brought into
winter quarters where the herbage is such that they can feed during the winter.

The whole reason the
reindeer were brought into that area is to afford food for the Eskimo, because they can live under the conditions that prevail in that part of the world.
Does the minister know whether they are herded in the land they come from?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes; I understand that the reindeer industry in Alaska is quite considerable. These reindeer were brought from Alaska; they were purchased from a corporation which was a large holder of reindeer in Alaska, and which, I understand, makes a business of shipping reindeer meat to points in the United States.
It is a Christmas delicacy sent to New York, and that sort of thing.

Government of the Yukon Territory-
Salaries and expenses connected with the administration of the territory, including surveys, $42,000.
Grant to the Yukon council for local purposes, the construction and maintenance of roads and such other expenditures as the

commissioner is authorized to expend by and with the advice and consent of the council or any committee thereof; and the accounts with respect to such expenditure shall be subject to examination and audit by the auditor general as provided by section 22, chapter 215, revised statutes, 1927, $70,000-Total, $112,000.

In connection with the old claims filed in the Yukon many years ago, has any machinery been set up by the department or through the gold commissioner by which these claims can be cleared away? Back in 1897-98, when the rush was on, thousands of claims were staked in the Yukon, some of which were proved up and then abandoned, or the people who owned them are dead to-day or have thrown them up. But with the increased price of gold another move is now starting into that part of the country. If the titles of those old claims are not cleared up it will be impossible for people to file on them again. Has anything been done by the department to clear up the claims staked at that time so that the ground can be staked now by newcomers?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think this is the first time this question has come to my attention.
There is one big company still operating.
Yes, the Tread-gold company. But there are many thousands of claims that might be staked again.
I saw their report not long since; they apparently did not make much money last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The information given to me is that the owners of these claims in many instances have moved away; the larger companies have been acquiring them, I assume, by purchase, and they are being operated by these larger companies.

But many claims that were staked there have been abandoned. The locators may have proved up or they may not, but as with certain oil leases, once claims are applied for and the fees paid they must go to public auction in order to be acquired by someone else.

I think the grants all contain provisions that certain operations have to be commenced within a given time, failure to do which empowers the crown to give notice cancelling the right, such as it is. The hon. member will perhaps remember the Poison case which went to the privy councilr that decided the validity of the notice, since-

Questions
which time the department has been very particular to give the notice in the manner prescribed by law. Once the notice is given the claim is cancelled.

I have in mind that there will be many pieces of ground which the prospectors may want to stake again and on which there has been no notice given. It is impossible for such claims to be restaked unless these old titles are cleared away.
I think the Yukon council now have power to clear the titles.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not think any difficulty should arise, because even if the owners have moved away these original claims are registered, and if a patent has been issued the authorities would not issue a new registration on a claim already held by someone else.

Many people
went in to the Yukon as prospectors, staked claims, proved up on them and possibly did not have enough money to carry on, or did not feel that it was a good enough stake, but to-day with the different price of gold it might be a good enough stake. Now, if such a man has died leaving no heirs to take the claim over, there is a blank piece of ground that might be staked by another prospector, but under present conditions it cannot be staked. Is there no way of cleaning that up so that development can go on?

If a patent has issued, obviously the title to the property has passed to somebody else. If no patent has issued the claim may be terminated for non-working. There is either a grant or no grant. If there is a grant there is a patent; the property is dealt with as ordinary property because it belongs to the heirs, and we have no jurisdiction over it. If no patent has issued, there is nothing but a claim, which can be forfeited by reason of non-working, and it would then become available for restaking.
In view of the fact that it was not expected we should reach this item to-night, and as the hon. member for the Yukon (Mrs. Black) is not present and wishes to make some observations with respect to the item, perhaps the minister will let it stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Under the circumstances I shall be very glad to do so.
Item stands.
